days.title: AWS SDKs, Resilient Calls, and Data Serialization

concepts.heading: Calling AWS Services Through the SDK
concepts.body: Every AWS API is an HTTPS request signed with Signature Version 4, and the AWS SDKs wrap that work: they build the request, sign it with credentials found through the default credential provider chain, send it, parse the response and raise typed exceptions. Credentials come from, in order, explicit code settings, environment variables, the shared config and credentials files, and finally the role attached to the compute (Lambda execution role, ECS task role, EC2 instance profile), so the same code runs on a laptop with a profile and in production with a role. Create clients once, outside the Lambda handler, so warm invocations reuse connections. Use paginators for List and Query calls that return a NextToken or LastEvaluatedKey, and waiters (for example a waiter for a table to become ACTIVE) instead of hand-written polling loops. A question showing hardcoded access keys is almost always solved with a role.

concepts.heading: Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
concepts.body: Transient failures such as HTTP 500, 503, 429 or ThrottlingException often succeed if you wait and try again. AWS SDKs retry these automatically with exponential backoff (each wait is longer than the last) plus random jitter, so thousands of clients recovering from the same blip do not retry in lockstep. You tune it instead of writing loops: in boto3, Config(retries={'mode': 'standard', 'max_attempts': 5}); the adaptive mode also rate-limits the client when it is being throttled. Client errors such as 400 ValidationException or 403 AccessDenied are not retried, because the same request will fail the same way. On the exam, sporadic throttling that clears by itself points to backoff with jitter or to raising the attempt count, never to an immediate tight retry loop, which adds load exactly when the service is already saturated.

concepts.heading: Idempotency Makes Retries Safe
concepts.body: A retry is only safe if repeating the request cannot cause a second side effect. When a client times out it cannot know whether the first attempt succeeded, so a payment or order API must be idempotent: the same request processed twice gives the same result once. The usual pattern is a client-generated idempotency key, such as a UUID, sent with the request; the server records processed keys, for example with a DynamoDB conditional PutItem using attribute_not_exists(pk), and returns the stored result for a repeat. Several AWS APIs accept a token for this, such as ClientRequestToken on DynamoDB TransactWriteItems. Consumers of SQS standard queues, SNS and EventBridge also need idempotency because those services deliver at least once. When a scenario mentions duplicate charges or duplicate records after retries, the answer is an idempotency key, not disabling retries.

concepts.heading: Graceful Degradation and Fault Tolerance
concepts.body: A resilient application keeps serving something useful when a dependency is slow or down, instead of failing completely. Set explicit client timeouts so a hung call does not consume the whole Lambda timeout, then fall back: serve a cached or default value, hide a non-critical widget such as recommendations, or queue the work for later and return HTTP 202 Accepted. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing for a cooling-off period, which protects both sides and lets you fail fast. Bulkheads (separate pools or reserved concurrency per dependency) keep one slow integration from starving others. For example, a product page can render without its reviews section when the reviews service times out after 500 ms. Exam answers that describe fallbacks, timeouts and queuing beat answers that simply add more retries to a dependency that is already failing.

concepts.heading: Serialization: JSON, Base64, and DynamoDB Marshalling
concepts.body: Application objects must be serialized into the format each AWS API expects and deserialized on the way back. Most payloads are JSON: a Lambda event arrives as a parsed object, but an API Gateway proxy event's body is a string you must JSON.parse, and the proxy response body must be a string too. Binary data travels base64-encoded: Kinesis record data in a Lambda event, binary API Gateway payloads and Bedrock image inputs in InvokeModel bodies. DynamoDB's low-level API uses typed AttributeValues, for example {"id": {"S": "A-1"}, "qty": {"N": "5"}}, where numbers are sent as strings. Higher-level helpers marshall native types for you: the DynamoDB DocumentClient or marshall/unmarshall in @aws-sdk/util-dynamodb, and the boto3 Table resource, which returns numbers as Python Decimal. Garbled records or type errors in a scenario usually point to a missing decode or unmarshall step.

examPoints: A question where calls fail intermittently with throttling or 5xx errors that succeed moments later is testing SDK retries with exponential backoff and jitter (standard or adaptive mode), not tight retry loops or disabling retries.

A scenario where retries create duplicate orders or charges is testing idempotency keys and conditional writes, because at-least-once delivery and client timeouts make duplicates unavoidable otherwise.

A question showing unreadable Kinesis data, a failed JSON parse of an API Gateway body, or DynamoDB items full of {"S": ...} wrappers is testing base64 decoding, JSON serialization and DynamoDB marshalling.

quiz.q: A Lambda function reads an item with the low-level DynamoDB GetItem API and passes it to a reporting library, which fails because every attribute arrives wrapped in objects such as {"S": "Seoul"} and {"N": "42"}. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Convert the item with the SDK's unmarshall helper or use the DocumentClient, which returns native strings and numbers
Store every attribute as a JSON string in a single String attribute so that the item never contains type descriptors
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode, because provisioned tables return items in the typed AttributeValue format
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the NEW_IMAGE view type and read the item from the stream record instead of the table
quiz.explain: The low-level API returns typed AttributeValues, and the unmarshall helper or a document client converts them to native types with no schema change. Choice B throws away the item's structure and makes queries on attributes impossible, and stream records use the same typed format anyway.

quiz.q: During a sale, an order service that calls a downstream inventory API sees bursts of HTTP 429 responses. The team wants requests to succeed without overloading the API further, and a retried order must never be created twice. Which combination should the developer implement?
choices: Retry each failed request immediately up to ten times, and log every duplicate order so that it can be cancelled later
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and send a client-generated idempotency key that the API uses to deduplicate
Disable SDK retries so that duplicates cannot happen, and return an error to the customer whenever a 429 is received
Increase the Lambda function's memory and timeout so that each request waits long enough for the inventory API to respond
quiz.explain: Backoff with jitter spreads retries out until capacity returns, and the idempotency key lets the server recognize a repeat of an order it already processed. Choice A retries in a tight loop, which adds load during throttling and cleans up duplicates only after they happen.

days.recap: Let the SDK sign, paginate and retry with backoff and jitter, make every retried write idempotent, degrade gracefully with timeouts and fallbacks, and serialize data the way each API expects (JSON strings, base64, typed DynamoDB attributes).

days.title: API Gateway: API Types, Validation, Transformations, Caching, and Throttling

concepts.heading: REST APIs vs HTTP APIs
concepts.body: API Gateway offers two kinds of RESTful API. REST APIs have the full feature set: request validators and models, mapping templates, response caching, API keys and usage plans, AWS WAF integration, private APIs reachable only through a VPC endpoint, and mock integrations. HTTP APIs are cheaper and lower latency and cover the common case of proxying to Lambda or an HTTP backend; they include native JWT authorizers, simple CORS and parameter mapping, but no caching, no usage plans and no request body validation. WebSocket APIs handle long-lived two-way connections. The exam usually decides the type through one feature in the stem: if the scenario needs caching, per-client quotas with API keys, WAF or schema validation of the body, choose a REST API; if it needs a simple, low-cost Lambda proxy with JWT authentication, choose an HTTP API.

concepts.heading: Proxy and Non-Proxy Integrations
concepts.body: With a Lambda proxy integration API Gateway passes the whole request (path, headers, query string, body as a string) to the function and expects a response object back with statusCode, headers and a string body; a malformed response object produces a 502 Bad Gateway. With a non-proxy (custom) integration, API Gateway transforms the request before calling the backend and transforms the response afterwards, using mapping templates. AWS service integrations call an AWS API directly, for example SQS SendMessage or DynamoDB PutItem, with no Lambda function in between, which removes code and cold starts for simple writes. HTTP integrations forward to another endpoint, and mock integrations return a fixed response without any backend. A scenario asking to put messages on a queue from an API without writing code points to an AWS service integration with a mapping template.

concepts.heading: Request Validation and Mapping Templates
concepts.body: A REST API can reject bad requests before they cost a backend invocation. A request validator checks that required query strings and headers exist, and a model (a JSON Schema) checks the body; failures return 400 Bad Request and the backend never runs. Mapping templates, written in Velocity Template Language (VTL), reshape payloads in non-proxy integrations: $input.path('$.order.id') extracts a field, $input.json('$') re-serializes the body, $util.escapeJavaScript and $util.base64Encode transform values, and $context.requestId adds request metadata. A response mapping template can rename fields or hide internal ones, and gateway responses customize errors such as the body of a 403 from an authorizer. HTTP APIs offer simpler parameter mapping that adds, overwrites or removes headers, query strings and paths. Questions about enforcing a schema without changing backend code point to models and validators.

concepts.heading: Response Caching
concepts.body: A REST API stage can enable a cache so repeated identical requests are answered from API Gateway without invoking the backend, lowering latency and cost. The TTL defaults to 300 seconds and can be set up to 3600 seconds, or 0 to disable caching for a method. The cache key is the resource path plus any query string parameters and headers you mark as cache keys; forget to include a parameter such as ?lang= and users receive each other's language. Per-method settings can turn caching off for write methods and endpoints with personalized data. Clients can invalidate an entry by sending Cache-Control: max-age=0; turn on Require authorization (an execute-api:InvalidateCache policy) so that only permitted callers can, because otherwise any client can flush entries. The cache is billed per hour by size. A read-heavy catalog endpoint that changes rarely is the classic caching answer; a per-user dashboard is not.

concepts.heading: Throttling and Usage Plans
concepts.body: API Gateway throttles with a token bucket: a steady-state rate in requests per second and a burst capacity. By default the account-level limit in most Regions is 10,000 requests per second with a burst of 5,000 (some newer Regions start lower), shared by all APIs, and you can set lower stage-level and method-level limits to protect a fragile backend. Requests over the limit receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, which clients should retry with backoff. For per-client control, a REST API usage plan links API keys to a throttle rate, burst and an optional quota such as 10,000 requests per day, so one partner's runaway integration is limited without affecting other callers. API keys identify clients for metering; they are not an authentication mechanism, so combine them with an authorizer. Throttling one noisy partner points to usage plans; protecting the whole backend points to stage or method throttling.

examPoints: A question that needs caching, usage plans with API keys, AWS WAF or JSON Schema body validation is testing that only REST APIs have these features, while HTTP APIs are the cheaper choice for a simple Lambda proxy with JWT auth.
A scenario where malformed payloads reach the backend, or where a field must be renamed without code changes, is testing request validators with models and VTL mapping templates.
A question about one partner's traffic causing 429s for everyone is testing usage plans and API keys, while stale or cross-user cached responses point to cache key parameters and TTL.

quiz.q: A REST API proxies to a Lambda function that crashes when the JSON body is missing the customerId field or when quantity is not an integer. The team wants these requests rejected before the function is invoked, with no change to the function code. What should the developer configure?
choices: An HTTP API with parameter mapping that removes requests without a customerId header before they reach the Lambda integration
A usage plan with an API key and a low burst limit, so that clients sending malformed bodies are throttled before they reach the function
A model that defines the body as a JSON Schema and a request validator for the method that validates the request body
A response mapping template that replaces the function's error output with a 400 status code and a friendly validation message
quiz.explain: A model plus a body request validator makes API Gateway check the schema and return 400 without invoking the backend. Choice D only rewrites the response after the function has already run and failed, so the bad request still reaches the code.

quiz.q: A REST API serves a product catalog whose data changes once an hour. The developer enables stage caching with a 300-second TTL, and users soon report seeing product descriptions in the wrong language, which is selected with the lang query string parameter. What should the developer do?
choices: Reduce the cache TTL to 30 seconds so that entries in the wrong language expire before most users notice them
Mark the lang query string parameter as a cache key on the method so that each language is cached separately
Disable caching and add a usage plan, because API Gateway caches cannot vary responses by query string values
Require clients to send Cache-Control: max-age=0 on every request so that the cache is always refreshed for them
quiz.explain: The cache key includes only the parameters marked as cache keys, so adding lang caches each language separately while keeping the hit rate. Choice A only shortens how long the wrong-language entry is served, and users would still get each other's language within the TTL.

days.recap: Pick REST APIs when you need validation, caching, usage plans or WAF and HTTP APIs for cheap Lambda proxies; validate with models, reshape with VTL mapping templates, cache with the right keys and TTL, and throttle per client with usage plans.

days.title: Decoupling and Event-Driven Patterns: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and S3 Events

concepts.heading: Tight vs Loose Coupling, Sync vs Async
concepts.body: In a tightly coupled system, one component calls another directly and waits, so a slow or failed consumer immediately slows or breaks the producer. Loose coupling puts a durable intermediary, such as a queue, topic or event bus, between them, so each side scales, fails and deploys independently. Choose synchronous request-response, for example API Gateway invoking Lambda, when the caller needs the answer now and the work is short; REST API integrations time out after 29 seconds by default. Choose asynchronous processing when the caller only needs an acknowledgement: the API puts the job on an SQS queue, returns HTTP 202 with a job ID, and a worker processes it at its own pace while the client polls or is notified later. Long-running video processing behind an API, or a producer that must not be blocked by an unreliable consumer, are strong signals for an asynchronous design.

concepts.heading: Amazon SQS Work Queues
concepts.body: SQS stores messages until a consumer receives and deletes them, which buffers bursts and protects a slower consumer. While a consumer processes a message it is hidden for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours); if the consumer does not delete it in time, the message becomes visible again and is retried, so set the timeout longer than the processing time. A redrive policy moves a message to a dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount failed receives. Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering; FIFO queues preserve order within a message group ID and deduplicate within a 5-minute window using a deduplication ID or content-based deduplication. Long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20) cuts empty responses and cost. Because each message is processed by one consumer, SQS alone does not broadcast an event to several systems.

concepts.heading: SNS Fan-Out and Message Filtering
concepts.body: Amazon SNS is publish-subscribe: a producer publishes once to a topic, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscription, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTPS endpoints, email or mobile push. The fan-out pattern subscribes one SQS queue per downstream system to a topic, so an order-placed event reaches inventory, billing and analytics independently; if analytics is down, its messages wait in its own queue and the others are unaffected. Subscription filter policies let each subscriber receive only matching messages, for example {"eventType": ["refund"]} on message attributes or, with payload-based filtering, on the message body, without the publisher knowing about subscribers. SNS FIFO topics paired with SQS FIFO queues keep ordering and deduplication across the fan-out. When a scenario says one event must drive several independent consumers that must not affect each other, think SNS to multiple SQS queues.

concepts.heading: Amazon EventBridge Event Routing
concepts.body: EventBridge is a serverless event bus that routes JSON events by content. Events arrive from AWS services on the default bus, from your code through PutEvents on a custom bus, or from SaaS partners on partner buses. Rules match event patterns on any field, for example {"source": ["orders"], "detail": {"amount": [{"numeric": [">", 1000]}]}}, and send matches to up to five targets per rule, such as Lambda, SQS, Step Functions or another bus, optionally reshaped by an input transformer. Archive and replay lets you re-send past events after fixing a consumer, and the schema registry can generate code bindings for event types. EventBridge Scheduler runs one-time or recurring invocations of targets. Choose EventBridge over SNS when routing depends on event content from many sources or SaaS applications; choose SNS for very high fan-out to known subscribers and SMS, email or push.

concepts.heading: Amazon S3 Event Notifications
concepts.body: S3 can emit an event when objects are created, removed, restored or replicated, which starts most upload-then-process pipelines, such as making a thumbnail after an image upload. Classic notifications send to a Lambda function, an SQS queue or an SNS topic, filtered by key prefix and suffix such as uploads/ and .jpg; overlapping prefix and suffix rules for the same event type are not allowed. Alternatively, enable EventBridge on the bucket and every event goes to the default bus, where rules can filter on object size, key patterns and more, and route to many targets. Delivery is at least once and usually within seconds, so handlers must be idempotent. A classic trap is a function that writes its output back to the same bucket and prefix that triggers it, creating a recursive loop; write to a different bucket or prefix.

examPoints: A question where a slow or failing consumer must not block the producer, or a long job sits behind an API, is testing asynchronous decoupling with SQS and an HTTP 202 response instead of a synchronous call.

A scenario where one event must independently trigger several systems is testing SNS fan-out to one SQS queue per consumer, while content-based routing from many sources or SaaS partners is testing EventBridge rules.
A question about processing every uploaded object, filtering by prefix and suffix, or an upload loop that never ends is testing S3 Event Notifications and the recursion trap.

quiz.q: An e-commerce platform must route events from its own services and from two SaaS partners to different Lambda functions, depending on fields inside each event such as region and order amount. New routes are added often, and producers must not change when a route is added. Which design fits best?
choices: An SNS standard topic per event source, with a subscription filter policy on message attributes added for each new Lambda route
A single SQS standard queue that all producers write to, with a Lambda consumer that inspects each message and calls the right function
A synchronous API Gateway endpoint per route, which the producers call directly with the event as the request body
An EventBridge custom bus plus partner event sources, with one rule per route whose event pattern matches the event content
quiz.explain: EventBridge accepts SaaS partner events natively and routes by patterns on any field of the event, so new rules need no producer change. Choice B re-creates routing in custom code, couples all routes to one consumer and lets one failure delay every route.

quiz.q: A Lambda function is triggered by s3:ObjectCreated events on the bucket media-in with no prefix filter. It resizes each image and writes the result to media-in/resized/. After deployment, the function's invocations grow without stopping and costs spike. What should the developer do?
choices: Write the resized images to a different bucket or prefix, and restrict the notification to an input prefix such as uploads/
Increase the function's reserved concurrency so that it can keep up with the volume of new events generated by uploads
Switch the notification to deliver through an SQS standard queue, which removes duplicate events before the function runs
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that overwriting the resized image does not generate another creation event
quiz.explain: Each output object is itself a new object in the watched bucket, which triggers the function again in a loop; writing elsewhere or filtering the notification on an input prefix breaks the cycle. Choice B lets the loop run faster and cost more.

days.recap: Decouple with durable intermediaries: SQS for work queues and async APIs, SNS for fan-out to independent queues, EventBridge for content-based routing from many sources, and S3 notifications for object-driven pipelines with idempotent, non-recursive handlers.

days.title: Streaming Data: Kinesis Data Streams, Data Firehose, and Lambda Consumers

concepts.heading: Kinesis Data Streams: Shards and Partition Keys
concepts.body: Kinesis Data Streams ingests ordered records that many consumers can read independently and replay, which is the difference from SQS, where one consumer deletes each message. A stream is made of shards. In provisioned mode each shard accepts up to 1 MB per second or 1,000 records per second of writes and serves 2 MB per second of reads; on-demand mode scales shards for you. A producer sends PutRecord or PutRecords with a partition key; Kinesis hashes the key to choose a shard, and records with the same key stay in order within that shard. Data is retained for 24 hours by default and can be extended up to 365 days. Pick keys with many distinct values, such as a device ID; a key like the date sends everything to one hot shard and causes ProvisionedThroughputExceededException even when the stream has spare shards.

concepts.heading: Producers, Throttling, and Ordering
concepts.body: PutRecords sends up to 500 records per call and is not all-or-nothing: the response has FailedRecordCount and a per-record ErrorCode, so code must resend only the failed records, with backoff. ProvisionedThroughputExceededException means a shard's write limit was hit; the fixes are better key distribution, more shards (resharding or on-demand mode) and retries with backoff. Ordering is guaranteed only per shard, so if all events for one order must be processed in sequence, use the order ID as the partition key. Each record gets a sequence number that is unique and increasing within its shard. The Kinesis Producer Library can aggregate small user records into larger Kinesis records to use shard capacity efficiently, and the consumer side must de-aggregate them. A stem where only some records in a batch are lost points to unhandled partial failures in PutRecords.

concepts.heading: Consumers: Shared Throughput, Enhanced Fan-Out, and KCL
concepts.body: Standard consumers poll with GetRecords and share each shard's 2 MB per second of read throughput, so adding a fourth or fifth application slows them all. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB per second per shard, pushed over HTTP/2 with SubscribeToShard, which lowers latency when several applications read the same stream. The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) handles shard discovery, balancing shards across workers and checkpointing progress in a DynamoDB lease table, so a restarted worker resumes from its last checkpoint. A consumer that falls behind shows a growing GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds metric; if it approaches the retention period, records will expire before they are read. When a scenario describes several independent applications that each need the full stream with low latency, the answer is enhanced fan-out, not more shards.

concepts.heading: Lambda as a Stream Consumer
concepts.body: Lambda reads Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams through an event source mapping that polls each shard and invokes the function with batches. Settings that matter: batch size and batching window (MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds) to trade latency for fewer invocations; starting position TRIM_HORIZON, LATEST or AT_TIMESTAMP; and a parallelization factor of up to 10 concurrent batches per shard while ordering is kept per partition key. Records arrive with the data base64-encoded, so the handler decodes event.Records[i].kinesis.data before parsing JSON. By default a failing batch is retried until it succeeds or the data expires, blocking that shard. Configure BisectBatchOnFunctionError, MaximumRetryAttempts, MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds, an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue, and ReportBatchItemFailures so only the failed record and its successors are retried. A stuck shard with rising iterator age points to these error-handling settings.

concepts.heading: Amazon Data Firehose for Managed Delivery
concepts.body: Amazon Data Firehose is the no-code way to load streaming data into destinations: Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Splunk, Apache Iceberg tables and generic HTTP endpoints. Producers write to a Firehose stream directly with PutRecord or PutRecordBatch, or Firehose reads from a Kinesis data stream as its source. Firehose buffers data by size and time before each delivery, so it is near real time rather than per-record; it can invoke a Lambda function to transform records, convert JSON to Apache Parquet or ORC using a Glue Data Catalog schema, compress output, and back up failed records to S3. You write no consumer, manage no shards and pay for data volume. Choose Firehose when the requirement is to land a stream in S3 or an analytics store with minimal code; choose Data Streams with custom consumers for sub-second processing, replay or multiple custom readers.

examPoints: A question with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException while other shards are idle, or with out-of-order events for one entity, is testing partition key choice: high cardinality for spread, and the entity ID as key for per-entity ordering.

A scenario where several applications read one stream and slow each other down is testing enhanced fan-out, while a Lambda consumer stuck on one bad record is testing bisect, retry limits, on-failure destinations and ReportBatchItemFailures.
A requirement to deliver streaming data to S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with transformation and format conversion but no consumer code is testing Amazon Data Firehose.

quiz.q: IoT devices send telemetry to a Kinesis data stream with 20 shards, using the current date as the partition key. Producers receive ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, but CloudWatch shows that 19 shards receive almost no writes. What should the developer change?
choices: Double the number of shards with UpdateShardCount so that the stream has twice the total write capacity available
Switch the producers from PutRecords to PutRecord so that each record is written to the stream in its own request
Register an enhanced fan-out consumer for each application that reads the stream so that read throughput increases
Use a high-cardinality partition key such as the device ID so that records are spread across all of the shards
quiz.explain: One date value hashes to a single shard, so every write lands on one hot shard; a device ID spreads records across all 20 shards. Choice A adds shards that the single key would still never use, so the hot shard stays throttled.

quiz.q: A Lambda function consumes a Kinesis data stream. One malformed record makes the function throw an error, and the function's iterator age for that shard keeps growing while the same batch is retried. The team wants healthy records to keep flowing and wants bad records kept for analysis. Which configuration meets this?
choices: Increase the batch size to 10,000 and the function timeout to 15 minutes so that each batch has enough time to finish
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures, split batches on error, limit retry attempts, and set an SQS on-failure destination
Configure a dead-letter queue on the function's asynchronous invocation settings and set the retry attempts to zero
Change the starting position to LATEST so that the event source mapping skips the record that keeps failing
quiz.explain: Partial batch responses, bisecting, a retry limit and an on-failure destination let the shard move past the bad record while its metadata is kept. Choice C configures asynchronous invocation, which does not apply to stream event source mappings, so the shard stays blocked.

days.recap: Spread Kinesis writes with high-cardinality partition keys, handle partial PutRecords failures, use enhanced fan-out for many low-latency readers, give Lambda stream consumers bisect and failure destinations, and use Firehose to land streams in storage without code.

days.title: AI in Application Development: Kiro, Amazon Bedrock APIs, and Knowledge Bases

concepts.heading: Spec-Driven Development, Steering, and Hooks in Kiro
concepts.body: Kiro is an AI-powered development environment from AWS built around spec-driven development: before the agent writes code, a feature is described in reviewable files under .kiro/specs/<feature>/. requirements.md holds user stories with acceptance criteria such as 'WHEN a user exports orders THE SYSTEM SHALL ...', design.md holds the technical design, and tasks.md lists implementation tasks linked to the requirements they satisfy. The team reviews and edits these before coding, and when requirements change they update the spec first so it stays the source of truth. Steering files in .kiro/steering/ give the agent standing project knowledge, such as 'use AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 clients', and are committed so every developer gets them. Agent hooks run an agent action on an IDE event, for example updating tests whenever a file under src/handlers is saved. Exam stems map plan-first traceability to specs, shared conventions to steering, and event-driven automation to hooks.

concepts.heading: Reviewing AI-Generated Code
concepts.body: AI tools generate, complete, refactor and review code, but their output must be treated as untrusted input. Generated code can build SQL or shell commands by string concatenation, hardcode example secrets, request IAM policies with bedrock:* on Resource '*', or target outdated APIs, such as require('aws-sdk') on a Lambda Node.js runtime that ships only the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3. It can even import packages that do not exist, which attackers then register. Safe practice combines human review with automated gates: static analysis, secret detection and dependency scanning run in CI and block the merge, IAM Access Analyzer validates generated policies, and dependencies come through a controlled repository such as AWS CodeArtifact. AI review findings are posted as pull request comments for humans to judge, not used as the merge decision. Refactoring suggestions are applied after characterization tests capture current behavior, in small tested steps.

concepts.heading: Calling Models: InvokeModel vs Converse
concepts.body: The bedrock-runtime client offers two styles of inference. InvokeModel sends a body in the model provider's native JSON format, so switching models means rewriting request and response handling. The Converse API uses one message format for all supporting models: messages with user and assistant roles, a system prompt, inferenceConfig for common parameters (maxTokens, temperature, topP, stopSequences) and additionalModelRequestFields for model-specific ones such as top_k. Converse also standardizes tool use: the model returns stopReason tool_use with a toolUse block, your code runs the tool, and you send back a toolResult with the matching toolUseId. Converse is stateless, so the application stores conversation history, for example in DynamoDB, and resends prior turns on every call. IAM uses the base actions: Converse needs bedrock:InvokeModel. ThrottlingException is handled with SDK backoff and, where allowed, a cross-Region inference profile such as us.<model-id>.

concepts.heading: Streaming Responses and Batch Inference
concepts.body: Chat interfaces should show text as it is generated. ConverseStream (or InvokeModelWithResponseStream) returns an event stream of messageStart, many contentBlockDelta events, messageStop with the stopReason and metadata with token usage. It is authorized by bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so a role with only InvokeModel gets AccessDeniedException after switching to streaming. To reach the browser, the backend must stream too: a Lambda function URL in RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode, or an API Gateway REST API whose response transfer mode is STREAM instead of the default BUFFERED. At the other extreme, large non-urgent jobs such as summarizing 60,000 tickets overnight belong in batch inference: JSONL files in S3 with recordId and modelInput per line, a CreateModelInvocationJob call, and output files joined back by recordId. Batch inference costs less than on-demand for supported models and removes your own throttling logic.

concepts.heading: Knowledge Bases and Amazon Quick
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases implement retrieval-augmented generation: documents from a source such as S3 are chunked, embedded and stored in a vector store, and queries retrieve relevant chunks to ground the model's answer. The bedrock-agent-runtime client offers Retrieve, which returns chunks for your own prompt, and RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns a generated answer with citations. For follow-up questions, pass back the sessionId that the first RetrieveAndGenerate response returned; you cannot invent your own. Agents you build are hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and called with InvokeAgentRuntime and a unique runtimeSessionId per conversation. Amazon Quick is an AI-powered service for business users: chat, agents, research and workflow automation over company data, connected through knowledge bases, action connectors, MCP or OpenAPI. A developer meets it as a consumer of the application's data and APIs, not as an SDK for app features (its Quick Sight BI feature is out of scope).

examPoints: A Kiro question is testing which feature fits: specs for reviewable plans and traceability, steering files for shared conventions, and agent hooks for actions triggered by events such as saving a file.
A scenario that lets AI-generated code or policies merge on green unit tests is testing human review plus automated scanning, least-privilege policy validation and dependency verification.

A Bedrock coding question is usually testing Converse request fields, its statelessness, streaming end to end with ConverseStream and the matching IAM action, batch inference for bulk jobs, or the sessionId for multi-turn RetrieveAndGenerate.

quiz.q: A Lambda function calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and works. The developer switches to ConverseStream and returns the result through an API Gateway REST API with a Lambda proxy integration in its default configuration. Every call now fails with AccessDeniedException. Which change fixes the error?
choices: Change the REST API integration's response transfer mode from BUFFERED to STREAM so that API Gateway accepts streamed data
Add bedrock:ConverseStream to the execution role, because each Bedrock Runtime operation is authorized by its own IAM action
Add bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the model ARN to the execution role, because that action authorizes ConverseStream
Request access to the streaming variant of the model in the Bedrock console, because streaming access is granted separately
quiz.explain: ConverseStream is authorized by bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, which the role lacks. Choice A is needed to stream to the browser later, but transfer mode cannot cause an IAM AccessDeniedException from Bedrock.

quiz.q: A team uses Kiro on a shared repository. Developers keep retyping the same rules into agent chats: use the SDK v3 modular clients, log structured JSON, and never hardcode Regions. The team wants every developer's agent to follow these rules in every session. What should the team do?
choices: Write the rules in markdown steering files under .kiro/steering and commit them so every developer's agent loads them
Create an agent hook that rewrites every saved file to match the rules, so mistakes are corrected after the developer saves
Add the rules as a final task in each feature's tasks.md so the agent applies them after implementing the rest of the spec
Rely on the agent to learn the rules from existing code, because the agent keeps conventions permanently after one session
quiz.explain: Steering files give the agent persistent shared project context, and committing them gives every developer the same rules. Choice B reacts after code is written and churns files instead of guiding generation up front.

days.recap: Use Kiro specs, steering and hooks for structured AI-assisted development, review and scan everything AI generates, call Bedrock with Converse (stateless, standardized, tool use), stream end to end or batch for bulk, and ground answers with Knowledge Bases.

days.title: Lambda Configuration and VPC Access

concepts.heading: Handler, Runtime, and the Execution Environment
concepts.body: A Lambda function's handler setting names the entry point the runtime calls for each event, for example app.handler for a Node.js file app.mjs exporting handler, or lambda_function.lambda_handler in Python. The handler receives the event and a context object with the request ID and remaining time (context.getRemainingTimeInMillis()). The runtime, such as nodejs22.x, python3.13 or java21, determines the language version and the bundled SDK, and deprecated runtimes stop receiving patches, so upgrades are your job. Lambda runs each invocation in an execution environment that is reused while warm: code outside the handler runs once per environment during the init phase, which is where SDK clients, database connections and loaded configuration belong. With the default Lambda compute type, each environment handles one request at a time. A handler that cannot be found, a wrong file name or a module format mismatch shows up as Runtime.HandlerNotFound or an import error at the first invocation.

concepts.heading: Memory, Timeout, and Ephemeral Storage
concepts.body: Memory can be set from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, and Lambda allocates CPU in proportion, so a CPU-bound function often runs faster and costs about the same or less with more memory, because billing is memory multiplied by duration. The timeout defaults to 3 seconds and can be raised to 900 seconds (15 minutes); work that needs longer belongs in Step Functions, ECS or a batch service, or in smaller chunks. Ephemeral storage in /tmp defaults to 512 MB and can be increased to 10,240 MB for functions that unpack large files. Watch the REPORT line in CloudWatch Logs: Max Memory Used close to the setting means risk of out-of-memory errors, and Duration close to the timeout means Task timed out errors. A scenario where a function times out calling a slow downstream API also suggests setting shorter client timeouts inside the code so the function can fail gracefully.

concepts.heading: Environment Variables, Layers, and Extensions
concepts.body: Environment variables pass configuration such as TABLE_NAME or LOG_LEVEL without code changes; together they are limited to 4 KB, are encrypted at rest by default, and can be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key instead. They are visible to anyone who can read the function configuration, so secrets belong in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, fetched at runtime and cached. Layers are .zip archives of libraries or a custom runtime extracted under /opt, shared across functions; a function can use up to five layers, and the unzipped function plus layers must stay within 250 MB. Extensions run alongside the function code through the Extensions API, for example monitoring agents or the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, which caches parameters and secrets and serves them to the handler on a localhost HTTP port, cutting API calls and latency. Extensions share the function's memory and can add init time.

concepts.heading: Concurrency Settings
concepts.body: Concurrency is the number of requests a function is processing at once, and all functions in a Region share an account quota (1,000 by default, raisable). Reserved concurrency guarantees a function that much of the pool and also caps it there, which protects a downstream database from too many connections; setting it to 0 stops all invocations, a useful emergency switch. Requests over the cap are throttled: synchronous callers receive a 429 TooManyRequestsException, and asynchronous events are retried. Provisioned concurrency keeps a number of environments initialized ahead of time on a version or alias, removing cold starts for latency-sensitive APIs at an extra cost, and Application Auto Scaling can schedule or track it. For SQS event sources, the event source mapping's maximum concurrency setting limits how many concurrent invocations one queue can drive. Stem phrases such as 'cap', 'protect the database' and 'cold start' map to these settings respectively.

concepts.heading: Connecting Lambda to a VPC
concepts.body: By default a function runs in a Lambda-managed VPC with internet access but cannot reach private resources such as an RDS instance or an ElastiCache cluster in your VPC. To reach them, configure the function with private subnets in at least two Availability Zones and a security group; Lambda creates Hyperplane elastic network interfaces, which requires ec2:CreateNetworkInterface, DescribeNetworkInterfaces and DeleteNetworkInterface permissions, provided by the AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole managed policy. The database's security group must allow inbound traffic from the function's security group. Once attached, the function has no internet access and no public IP, even in a public subnet. To call internet APIs, route the private subnets through a NAT gateway in a public subnet; to call AWS services privately, add gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB or interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for services such as Secrets Manager, SQS or Bedrock. Timeouts to AWS APIs after VPC attachment point to a missing route or endpoint.

examPoints: A question where a function times out on AWS API calls right after being attached to a VPC is testing that VPC functions need a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for outbound access, plus the ENI permissions and security group rules.
A scenario about protecting a database from too many connections or about cold-start latency is testing reserved concurrency versus provisioned concurrency.

A question about secrets in environment variables, shared libraries across functions, or a sidecar agent is testing Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, layers, and extensions such as the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension.

quiz.q: A Lambda function was moved into private subnets so it can query an Amazon RDS database. Queries now work, but calls to AWS Secrets Manager time out. The subnets have no NAT gateway, and security requires that traffic to AWS services stays off the internet. What should the developer do?
choices: Move the function into a public subnet so that it receives a public IP address and can reach the Secrets Manager endpoint
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager and add it to the route tables that the function's private subnets use
Increase the function's timeout to 900 seconds so that the request to Secrets Manager has enough time to complete
Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager with private DNS enabled and allow HTTPS from the function's security group
quiz.explain: An interface endpoint brings Secrets Manager into the VPC over PrivateLink, and private DNS lets the SDK use its normal hostname. Choice B fails because gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB.

quiz.q: A Lambda function writes to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance that supports at most 100 connections. During traffic spikes the function scales out and the database starts refusing connections. Which Lambda setting directly limits how many copies of the function can run at once?
choices: Provisioned concurrency set to 50 on the production alias, so that only 50 execution environments are ever created
Reserved concurrency set to a value below the database's connection limit, which caps concurrent executions
A larger memory setting so that each invocation finishes faster and fewer executions overlap during spikes
A longer timeout so that each invocation keeps its connection open and reuses it for more queued requests
quiz.explain: Reserved concurrency is both a guarantee and a hard cap on concurrent executions, so it bounds the number of connections. Choice A pre-warms environments but does not stop Lambda from scaling beyond them with on-demand concurrency.

days.recap: Initialize clients outside the handler, size memory and timeout from the REPORT line, keep secrets out of environment variables, share code with layers and agents with extensions, use reserved concurrency to cap and provisioned to pre-warm, and give VPC functions NAT or endpoints.

days.title: Lambda Event Lifecycles, Error Handling, and Service Integrations

concepts.heading: Three Ways Lambda Is Invoked
concepts.body: How errors are retried depends on the invocation type. Synchronous invocation (API Gateway, ALB, function URLs, the SDK with RequestResponse) waits for the result, and the caller sees the error and decides whether to retry; Lambda itself does not retry. Asynchronous invocation (S3, SNS, EventBridge, InvocationType Event) puts the event on an internal queue and returns 202 at once; Lambda retries a failed event up to two more times by default, and you can set retries from 0 to 2 and a maximum event age from 60 seconds to 6 hours. Event source mappings (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, Amazon MSK) are pollers that Lambda runs to read the source and invoke the function synchronously with batches; their retry behavior follows the source, such as SQS visibility timeouts or stream retry settings. On the exam, identify the invocation type first, because DLQs, destinations and batch settings each apply only to some types.

concepts.heading: Destinations and Dead-Letter Queues for Async Events
concepts.body: For asynchronous invocations you can capture events that still fail after all retries. A dead-letter queue on the function (an SQS queue or SNS topic) receives only the original event. Destinations are richer: an on-failure destination receives an invocation record with the event plus error details, the function's response and request context, and an on-success destination receives the result of successful runs, which lets you chain processing without code. Destination targets can be an SQS queue, SNS topic, another Lambda function, an EventBridge bus or, for failures only, an S3 bucket. Destinations are the better choice for new designs because they carry more context. The execution role needs permission to send to the target, for example sqs:SendMessage. Remember the scope: an SQS-triggered function does not use these async settings at all; for SQS sources, failures go to a redrive DLQ configured on the source queue after maxReceiveCount receives.

concepts.heading: SQS Event Source Mappings and Partial Batch Responses
concepts.body: With an SQS trigger, Lambda polls the queue, invokes the function with up to the batch size of messages, and deletes them when the function returns successfully. If the function throws, the whole batch becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and is retried, so successfully processed messages are processed twice. To avoid this, enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the mapping and return {"batchItemFailures": [{"itemIdentifier": messageId}]} listing only the failed messages; the rest are deleted. Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout, as AWS recommends, so messages are not redelivered while still being processed. A redrive policy with maxReceiveCount moves poison messages to a DLQ. Event filtering on the mapping can drop irrelevant messages before invocation, which saves cost. For FIFO queues, a failure stops processing of that message group until it succeeds or is moved to the DLQ.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Streams and Stream Triggers
concepts.body: DynamoDB Streams records item-level changes for 24 hours, in order per item, and a Lambda event source mapping can process them to update aggregates, send notifications or replicate data. The stream view type decides what each record contains: KEYS_ONLY, NEW_IMAGE, OLD_IMAGE or NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES, which you need to compare before and after values. Records arrive in the typed AttributeValue format, so unmarshall them before use. Like Kinesis, a failing batch blocks its shard until it succeeds or expires, so configure BisectBatchOnFunctionError, MaximumRetryAttempts, MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds, an on-failure destination and ReportBatchItemFailures. Event filters such as {"eventName": ["INSERT"]} invoke the function only for new items. The function's execution role needs dynamodb:GetRecords, GetShardIterator, DescribeStream and ListStreams on the stream. When an order status change must trigger an email without touching the writing code, the answer is a DynamoDB Streams trigger.

concepts.heading: Permissions and Integrations: Push vs Poll
concepts.body: Lambda permissions point in two directions. For push sources such as API Gateway, S3, SNS and EventBridge, the source invokes the function, so the function's resource-based policy must allow that service, added with lambda add-permission and a SourceArn condition; consoles add this automatically, but IaC templates often miss it, and the symptom is an event that never arrives. For event source mappings, Lambda reads the source itself, so the execution role needs read permissions such as sqs:ReceiveMessage and sqs:DeleteMessage. API Gateway proxy integrations require the function to return {statusCode, headers, body} with body as a string; otherwise clients receive 502. Inside the handler, code calls other services with the SDK, for example writing to DynamoDB, and on-success destinations or EventBridge can pass results onward. When a trigger configured in CloudFormation never fires but manual tests work, check the resource-based policy first.

examPoints: A question about failed events from S3, SNS or EventBridge is testing asynchronous retries, maximum event age, and on-failure destinations (with error context) versus a function DLQ (event only).

A scenario where successful SQS messages are processed again after one message fails is testing ReportBatchItemFailures with batchItemFailures, the visibility timeout and a redrive DLQ on the source queue.
A trigger that never fires when deployed through IaC is testing the function's resource-based policy for push sources, while an event source mapping that cannot read is testing the execution role.

quiz.q: A Lambda function processes SQS messages in batches of 10. When one message in a batch fails validation, the function throws an exception, and the nine valid messages are processed again later, creating duplicate records. What should the developer change?
choices: Set the batch size to 1 and raise the function's reserved concurrency so that every message is processed in its own invocation
Configure an on-failure destination in the function's asynchronous invocation settings so that the failed batch is moved aside
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and return only the failed message IDs in batchItemFailures
Reduce the queue's visibility timeout to zero so that the failed message is retried immediately while the others are deleted
quiz.explain: With partial batch responses, Lambda deletes the successful messages and returns only the listed ones to the queue. Choice B fails because asynchronous invocation settings do not apply to an SQS event source mapping, which invokes the function synchronously.

quiz.q: An S3 bucket triggers a Lambda function asynchronously. When the function fails, the operations team wants each failed event delivered to an SQS queue together with the error message and stack trace, so they can diagnose the failure without searching the logs. What should the developer configure?
choices: An on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations that points to the SQS queue, and sqs:SendMessage in the execution role
A dead-letter queue on the function that points to the SQS queue, because the DLQ message body includes the full invocation record
A redrive policy on the SQS queue with maxReceiveCount set to 2, so that failed events are moved there after two attempts
An event source mapping from the SQS queue to the function, with ReportBatchItemFailures enabled for failed S3 events
quiz.explain: An on-failure destination receives an invocation record with the event plus the error details and response context. Choice B fails because a function DLQ receives only the original event, without the error information the team needs.

days.recap: Know the invocation type first: sync callers retry themselves, async events get retries plus destinations or DLQs, and event source mappings follow the source with partial batch responses and bisecting; push sources need resource-based policies, pollers need execution role permissions.

days.title: DynamoDB for Developers: Keys, Indexes, Queries, Consistency, TTL, and DAX

concepts.heading: Designing Keys for Access Patterns
concepts.body: DynamoDB stores items by primary key: a partition key alone, or a partition key plus a sort key (composite key). The partition key is hashed to choose a physical partition, so it must have high cardinality and spread requests evenly; a status field with three values or the current date creates hot partitions and throttling even when table capacity looks sufficient. The sort key orders items within a partition and enables range queries, for example PK = CUSTOMER#123 and SK = ORDER#2026-10-01 to list one customer's orders by date with begins_with or between. Design keys from the queries the application must run, not from entities, because DynamoDB has no joins. For extremely hot keys, write sharding adds a random or calculated suffix such as CANDIDATE#7 to spread writes. Items are limited to 400 KB, so large payloads go to S3 with a pointer in the item.

concepts.heading: Local and Global Secondary Indexes
concepts.body: Secondary indexes add access patterns. A local secondary index (LSI) keeps the table's partition key with a different sort key, for example orders by amount instead of by date; it must be created with the table, supports strongly consistent reads, shares the table's capacity, and limits each partition key value's items to 10 GB. A table can have up to five LSIs. A global secondary index (GSI) can use a completely different partition and sort key, such as email to look up users, can be added or removed at any time, has its own capacity, and supports only eventually consistent reads. Projections decide which attributes are copied into an index: KEYS_ONLY, INCLUDE or ALL; querying an attribute not projected requires extra reads. A GSI without enough write capacity throttles writes to the base table. New access pattern on a live table means GSI; strong consistency on an alternate sort order means LSI.

concepts.heading: Query vs Scan
concepts.body: Query reads items for one partition key value, optionally narrowed by a sort key condition, and reads only those items, so it is efficient. Scan reads every item in the table or index and is expensive at scale. A FilterExpression on either operation is applied after items are read, so it reduces what is returned but not the capacity consumed. Results come in pages of up to 1 MB; when LastEvaluatedKey is present, pass it as ExclusiveStartKey to get the next page, or use an SDK paginator. ProjectionExpression returns only chosen attributes, saving bandwidth but not read capacity. When a Scan is unavoidable, such as a nightly export, parallel scan with Segment and TotalSegments spreads the work across workers, and a smaller Limit with pauses reduces impact on production traffic. A stem where a Scan with a filter is slow and costly usually wants a Query on a new GSI instead.

concepts.heading: Read Consistency and Capacity
concepts.body: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default: a read just after a write might return the previous value. Setting ConsistentRead to true returns the latest committed value, at twice the cost: one read capacity unit gives one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads. Strongly consistent reads are available on tables and LSIs but not on GSIs or DynamoDB Streams. One write capacity unit is one write per second of up to 1 KB, and transactional reads and writes cost double. Capacity mode can be on-demand (pay per request, no planning) or provisioned with auto scaling. Conditional writes such as ConditionExpression attribute_not_exists(pk) or version = :expected implement idempotent inserts and optimistic locking; a failed condition raises ConditionalCheckFailedException. Read-after-write requirements in a stem point to ConsistentRead on the table, never on a GSI.

concepts.heading: TTL and DynamoDB Accelerator
concepts.body: Time to Live deletes expired items without consuming write capacity. You choose an attribute, for example expiresAt, and store a Number holding a Unix epoch time in seconds; items whose time has passed are deleted in the background, typically within a few days, so queries should also filter out items that are expired but not yet deleted. A value in milliseconds or stored as a string is ignored. TTL deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions, so a stream consumer can archive expired session or cart items to S3. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory, write-through cache that is API-compatible with DynamoDB and cuts read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for read-heavy, repeated-key workloads. DAX serves eventually consistent reads; strongly consistent reads pass through to the table. It runs as a cluster in your VPC. Microsecond reads with minimal code change point to DAX.

examPoints: A question with throttling on a few keys while table capacity is available is testing high-cardinality partition keys and write sharding.
A scenario adding a new lookup to a live table is testing GSIs (any time, eventual consistency), while strong consistency on an alternate sort key created with the table is testing LSIs.

A question about a slow, expensive Scan with a FilterExpression, stale reads after writes, expired items still returned, or microsecond read latency is testing Query on an index, ConsistentRead, TTL behavior and DAX respectively.

quiz.q: A sessions table stores an expiresAt attribute as a String in ISO 8601 format, and TTL is enabled on that attribute. Weeks later, no sessions have been deleted. What should the developer do?
choices: Store expiresAt as a Number containing the expiry time as a Unix epoch timestamp in seconds
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table, because TTL deletes items only when a stream is attached
Add a GSI on expiresAt so that the TTL process can find expired items without scanning the table
Switch the table from provisioned to on-demand capacity, because TTL uses spare write capacity
quiz.explain: TTL only acts on a Number attribute holding epoch seconds, so ISO strings are ignored. Choice C misunderstands TTL, which needs no index; it scans in the background on its own and never consumes your capacity.

quiz.q: A user profile table has userId as its partition key. A new feature must look up profiles by email address, and the table already holds production data. Lookups after a profile update can tolerate a short delay. What is the most efficient solution?
choices: Scan the table with a FilterExpression on email for each lookup and cache the results in the application
Add a global secondary index with email as the partition key and Query the index for each lookup
Add a local secondary index with email as the sort key and query it with a strongly consistent read
Create a new table with email as the partition key and copy every item with a nightly batch job
quiz.explain: A GSI can be added to a live table with a different partition key, and its eventual consistency is acceptable here. Choice C fails because LSIs can only be created with the table and keep the userId partition key, so they cannot look up by email.

days.recap: Design keys from access patterns with high-cardinality partition keys, add GSIs for new lookups and LSIs only at creation, Query instead of Scan, use ConsistentRead when needed (not on GSIs), store TTL as epoch seconds, and add DAX for microsecond reads.

days.title: Choosing Data Stores, Caching Strategies, and Data Lifecycles

concepts.heading: Matching the Store to the Access Pattern
concepts.body: Choose a data store by how the data is read and written. Amazon S3 holds objects of any size, from images to data lake files, with eleven nines of durability, accessed by key; it is not a database to query row by row. DynamoDB serves key-value and document access at any scale with single-digit millisecond latency when the queries are known in advance. Amazon RDS and Aurora suit relational data that needs SQL joins, ad hoc queries, foreign keys and multi-row transactions, such as an order system with reporting. Amazon ElastiCache keeps data in memory for sub-millisecond reads of hot data, sessions or leaderboards. A useful exam approach is to underline the access words in the stem: 'ad hoc SQL' or 'joins' means relational, 'millions of requests per second by key' means DynamoDB, 'files' or 'objects' means S3, and 'sub-millisecond' or 'session store' means ElastiCache.

concepts.heading: Relational Databases for Developers
concepts.body: RDS runs engines such as PostgreSQL and MySQL; Aurora is the AWS-built compatible engine with storage replicated six ways across three Availability Zones. Read replicas offload reads, and Aurora gives a reader endpoint that load-balances across replicas while the cluster endpoint always points to the writer, so code should send writes to the cluster endpoint and reporting queries to the reader endpoint. Replicas are asynchronous, so a read just after a write might be stale. Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine-grained steps for spiky or unpredictable load. Lambda functions opening many short-lived connections can exhaust a database, so use RDS Proxy to pool and share connections, or the RDS Data API over HTTPS with IAM for Aurora. A Multi-AZ deployment is for availability, not for read scaling: its standby does not serve reads in the classic single-standby configuration.

concepts.heading: Caching Strategies: Lazy Loading vs Write-Through
concepts.body: Lazy loading (cache-aside) reads from the cache first and, on a miss, reads the database and writes the result into the cache with a TTL. Only requested data is cached and a cache failure is not fatal, but the first read of each key is slow and data can be stale until the TTL expires. Write-through updates the cache every time the application writes to the database, so cached data stays current, but every write pays the extra cost and the cache fills with data that may never be read. Most designs combine both: write-through for data that must be fresh, lazy loading for the rest, and a TTL on every key so stale or unused entries expire. For example, a product price might be written through on update and cached for 3600 seconds. A stem that complains about stale reads points to write-through or a shorter TTL; one about a cache full of unused data points to lazy loading.

concepts.heading: Picking the Right Cache for the Store
concepts.body: Each cache fits a different layer. DAX sits in front of DynamoDB and needs almost no code change, because its client speaks the DynamoDB API. ElastiCache (Valkey, Redis OSS or Memcached engines) caches anything: query results from RDS, computed objects, sessions and rate counters. Choose Valkey or Redis OSS for replication, persistence options, sorted sets for leaderboards and pub/sub; choose Memcached for a simple, multithreaded cache with no persistence. CloudFront caches static and dynamic HTTP content at edge locations close to users, typically in front of S3 or an API, and API Gateway caching answers repeated REST API requests at the stage. An application's own in-memory variables in a warm Lambda environment can cache small configuration. When a stem names DynamoDB plus microseconds, answer DAX; RDS plus repeated queries, ElastiCache; global static assets, CloudFront.

concepts.heading: Managing Data Lifecycles and Retention
concepts.body: Data should not live forever by accident. S3 Lifecycle rules transition objects between storage classes and expire them, for example moving logs/ objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90, and deleting them after 365; with versioning, NoncurrentVersionExpiration removes old versions, and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload cleans abandoned uploads. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects automatically when access patterns are unknown. S3 Object Lock retention (governance or compliance mode) and legal holds prevent deletion when rules require it. In DynamoDB, TTL expires items such as sessions, and in CloudWatch Logs each log group has a retention setting that defaults to never expire. RDS automated backups have a retention period of up to 35 days. A question about cost growing from old data points to lifecycle rules and retention settings; one about preventing deletion points to Object Lock.

examPoints: A question that describes access words such as joins, key lookups at massive scale, objects, or sub-millisecond reads is testing data store selection among RDS or Aurora, DynamoDB, S3 and ElastiCache.

A scenario about stale cached data or a cache full of unused entries is testing write-through versus lazy loading and TTLs, while the cache named in the answer must match the store (DAX for DynamoDB, ElastiCache for RDS, CloudFront for HTTP content).
A question about storage cost growing from old objects, versions, logs or items is testing S3 Lifecycle rules, log group retention and DynamoDB TTL.

quiz.q: An application caches product details in ElastiCache using lazy loading with a 24-hour TTL. When prices change in the Aurora database, customers see old prices for hours. Writes are infrequent, and prices must appear within seconds of a change. What should the developer do?
choices: Switch the cache to the Memcached engine, which checks the database for changes before it returns a cached value
Remove the TTL from all keys so that the cache never expires entries and always serves the most recent value
Add an Aurora read replica and send all product reads to the reader endpoint instead of to the cache cluster
Update or delete the cached entry whenever the application writes a new price, and keep a TTL as a safety net
quiz.explain: Writing through (or invalidating) on each price update keeps the cache current, and the TTL still limits staleness if an update is missed. Choice B makes the problem worse, because entries that are never refreshed stay stale forever.

quiz.q: An S3 bucket with versioning enabled stores application logs. Costs keep rising, although the team only queries the last 30 days of logs and must keep logs for one year. Which configuration best controls the cost?
choices: Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a one-year retention period on every log object in the bucket
Add a lifecycle rule that moves logs to colder storage after 30 days and expires all versions after one year
Suspend versioning on the bucket and delete objects older than 30 days with a scheduled Lambda function
Move the logs into a DynamoDB table with TTL set to one year, and query the last 30 days with a Scan operation
quiz.explain: A lifecycle rule moves rarely read logs to cheaper storage and expires both current and noncurrent versions after the retention period. Choice C deletes logs after 30 days, which breaks the one-year retention requirement.

days.recap: Pick the store from the access pattern, use RDS Proxy or reader endpoints for relational apps, combine lazy loading and write-through with TTLs, match the cache to the store, and control growth with lifecycle rules, TTL and retention settings.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Development with AWS Services

concepts.heading: Resilient Code and APIs Recap
concepts.body: Domain 1 starts with how code talks to AWS. The SDK signs requests with credentials from the provider chain, paginates, and retries throttling and 5xx errors with exponential backoff and jitter; your job is to make retried writes idempotent with keys and conditional writes, set timeouts, and degrade gracefully with fallbacks or queued work. Serialization questions hinge on JSON strings in API Gateway proxy bodies, base64 data in Kinesis records, and typed DynamoDB AttributeValues that need marshalling. For APIs, REST APIs bring validators, models, VTL mapping templates, caching, usage plans and WAF, while HTTP APIs are cheaper proxies with JWT authorizers. Cache keys and TTLs decide correctness of cached responses, and usage plans isolate one noisy client. If a stem names a feature only REST APIs have, that alone decides the API type.

concepts.heading: Messaging, Events, and Streams Recap
concepts.body: Decoupling questions ask whether the caller needs the answer now. If not, go asynchronous: SQS absorbs bursts with visibility timeouts and DLQs, SNS fans one event out to independent queues with filter policies, EventBridge routes by event content from AWS, custom and SaaS sources, and S3 Event Notifications start pipelines when objects arrive, with the recursion trap to avoid. Streaming questions focus on Kinesis Data Streams: partition keys with high cardinality spread load, the same key keeps per-entity order, enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own throughput, and PutRecords partial failures must be resent. Amazon Data Firehose lands streams in S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with buffering, Lambda transformation and format conversion but no consumer code. When the stem says 'replay' or 'multiple independent readers', think Data Streams rather than SQS.

concepts.heading: Lambda Recap
concepts.body: Lambda configuration questions test the handler and runtime, memory (128 MB to 10,240 MB with proportional CPU), the 15-minute timeout, /tmp size, environment variables (4 KB, no raw secrets), layers under /opt, and extensions such as the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension. Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees; provisioned concurrency pre-warms. VPC-attached functions need private subnets, a security group, ENI permissions, and a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for anything outside the VPC. Event lifecycle questions start with the invocation type: synchronous callers handle their own retries, asynchronous events get up to two retries plus destinations or a DLQ, and event source mappings follow the source, with ReportBatchItemFailures, bisecting and on-failure destinations for streams. Push sources need a resource-based policy; pollers need execution role permissions.

concepts.heading: Data Stores Recap
concepts.body: DynamoDB design starts with access patterns and a high-cardinality partition key, then adds GSIs for new lookups on live tables and LSIs only at creation for alternate sort keys with strong consistency. Query beats Scan, filters do not reduce consumed capacity, pages end with LastEvaluatedKey, ConsistentRead works on tables and LSIs only, and TTL needs epoch seconds in a Number attribute. DAX gives microsecond DynamoDB reads. Beyond DynamoDB, map access words to stores: relational joins to RDS or Aurora (with RDS Proxy for Lambda), objects to S3, sub-millisecond hot data to ElastiCache. Caching strategy is lazy loading for read efficiency, write-through for freshness, and TTLs on everything. Lifecycle questions are answered with S3 Lifecycle transitions and expirations, noncurrent version cleanup, log retention and TTL.

concepts.heading: AI-Assisted Development and AI Services Recap
concepts.body: The new C03 skills add AI to the developer's day. Kiro specs (requirements, design, tasks) make AI work reviewable and traceable before code is written, steering files share project conventions, and agent hooks automate follow-up work on events such as file saves. Everything AI generates, from code to IAM policies to dependencies, goes through human review and automated scanning before merge. For integrating Amazon Bedrock, use the Converse API for a model-independent message format, inferenceConfig and additionalModelRequestFields for parameters, application-side history because Converse is stateless, the toolUse and toolResult loop for tools, ConverseStream with InvokeModelWithResponseStream permission and a streaming Lambda response for live output, batch inference for bulk jobs, and Knowledge Bases RetrieveAndGenerate with the returned sessionId for grounded multi-turn answers.

examPoints: A Domain 1 question usually hides its answer in one requirement word: 'independently' (fan-out), 'by content' (EventBridge), 'replay' (Kinesis), 'without code' (service integrations or Firehose), 'cap' or 'cold start' (reserved or provisioned concurrency), 'new lookup' (GSI).
A question that mixes Lambda error handling with a specific event source is testing whether you apply the settings that belong to that invocation type, not the ones that sound similar.

quiz.q: A team's Lambda function, triggered by an Amazon Kinesis data stream, is attached to a VPC to write to an ElastiCache cluster. It must also put a summary into an Amazon Data Firehose stream. After VPC attachment, cache writes succeed but Firehose calls time out. The subnets are private with no NAT gateway. What should the developer add?
choices: An interface VPC endpoint for Amazon Data Firehose with private DNS enabled, reachable from the function's security group
An on-failure destination on the Kinesis event source mapping that sends timed-out batches to an SQS queue for later replay
A larger parallelization factor on the event source mapping so that more batches per shard run while Firehose calls wait
A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon Data Firehose added to the route tables of the private subnets that the function uses
quiz.explain: A VPC-attached function without NAT can reach AWS services only through VPC endpoints, and Firehose uses an interface endpoint. Choice D fails because gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

quiz.q: A chatbot backend calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API from Lambda with only the user's latest message. Users say the bot forgets what they said one message earlier. What should the developer do?
choices: Raise maxTokens in inferenceConfig so that the model keeps the earlier turns of the conversation in its context window
Pass a fixed session ID in each Converse request so that Bedrock stores the conversation history between separate calls
Store each conversation's turns, for example in DynamoDB, and send the prior user and assistant messages on every call
Enable provisioned concurrency on the function so that the same execution environment keeps the history in memory
quiz.explain: Converse is stateless, so the application must persist the history and resend prior turns in messages. Choice D fails because warm environments are not tied to a user and can disappear at any time, so memory is not a reliable conversation store.

days.recap: Domain 1 is about writing code that survives failures, choosing sync or async and the right messaging or streaming service, configuring Lambda for its invocation type, picking and caching data stores by access pattern, and integrating AI tools and Bedrock safely.

days.title: Authentication and Federation: Cognito, JWTs, MFA, and API Authorizers

concepts.heading: User Pools vs Identity Pools
concepts.body: Amazon Cognito has two parts that solve different problems. A user pool is a user directory and OpenID Connect identity provider: it handles sign-up, sign-in, password policies, MFA and account recovery, and after authentication it issues JSON Web Tokens: an ID token with identity claims, an access token with scopes for calling your APIs, and a refresh token to obtain new tokens. An identity pool (federated identities) exchanges a token from a user pool, a social provider, a SAML or OIDC provider, or even an unauthenticated guest for temporary AWS credentials from STS, tied to IAM roles. Use a user pool when users must log in to your app and call your API; add an identity pool when the client itself must call AWS services directly, such as uploading to S3 from a mobile app. A stem that says 'temporary AWS credentials for app users' means identity pool.

concepts.heading: Federating External Identity Providers
concepts.body: Identity federation lets users sign in with an identity they already have instead of a new password.
