A user pool can federate with social providers (Google, Facebook, Apple, Login with Amazon), with enterprise SAML 2.0 providers such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, and with any OpenID Connect provider. The user pool's managed login (hosted UI) redirects the user to the provider, receives the SAML assertion or OIDC token, maps attributes such as email into the user profile, and then issues its own user pool tokens, so your application validates one token format regardless of where the user came from. For AWS credentials, an identity pool can trust the user pool, or trust SAML and OIDC providers directly, and choose IAM roles with rules based on claims or groups. A stem asking to let corporate users sign in to a customer-facing app with their existing directory points to SAML federation in a user pool.

concepts.heading: MFA and Fine-Grained Access
concepts.body: Multi-factor authentication adds a second proof of identity. Cognito user pools support MFA through SMS text messages, email messages (Essentials or Plus feature plan, sent with your own Amazon SES configuration) and time-based one-time passwords (TOTP) from authenticator apps, configured as off, optional or required. Adaptive authentication, part of Cognito threat protection (formerly advanced security features, Plus plan), can require MFA only for risky sign-ins. Fine-grained authorization then decides what an authenticated user may do. User pool groups can map to IAM roles in an identity pool, and IAM policy variables restrict credentials to the user's own data, for example the condition dynamodb:LeadingKeys equal to ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} so each user reads only items whose partition key is their identity ID, or an S3 prefix per user. Scopes in the access token, such as orders/read, let an API allow specific operations. 'Each user may access only their own items' points to policy variables, not application filtering.

concepts.heading: Validating JWTs Correctly
concepts.body: A JWT is three base64url parts: header, payload with claims, and signature. Anyone can decode it, so never trust a token you have not verified. Correct validation checks the signature with the public key from the user pool's JWKS at https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<userPoolId>/.well-known/jwks.json, matching the kid in the header; then checks exp has not passed, iss equals the user pool URL, and the audience: aud for ID tokens or client_id for access tokens, plus token_use (id or access). Libraries such as aws-jwt-verify do all of this and cache the keys. Send access tokens to APIs, not ID tokens, unless the API was designed for ID tokens. Tokens expire (access and ID tokens are short-lived, refresh tokens longer), and revoking a refresh token stops new tokens. Decoding the payload without checking the signature is a classic wrong answer.

concepts.heading: API Gateway Authorizers
concepts.body: API Gateway can authenticate callers before the backend runs. A REST API Cognito user pool authorizer validates a user pool token in the Authorization header and can require OAuth scopes per method. An HTTP API JWT authorizer validates tokens from any OIDC issuer, Cognito included, by issuer and audience. A Lambda authorizer runs your code for custom schemes, such as a third-party token or an HMAC signature: a TOKEN authorizer receives one header, a REQUEST authorizer receives headers, query strings and context, and both return an IAM policy (or a simple boolean response for HTTP APIs) with optional context values, cached by TTL (300 seconds by default for REST APIs). IAM authorization requires SigV4-signed requests and suits service-to-service calls or clients holding identity pool credentials. Choose the managed authorizer when the token is from Cognito or a standard OIDC provider; choose a Lambda authorizer only for custom logic.

examPoints: A question about app users calling AWS services directly from a device is testing identity pools and temporary credentials, while user sign-in, MFA and tokens for your own API are testing user pools.

A scenario about corporate or social logins is testing user pool federation with SAML 2.0 or OIDC providers, and 'each user only their own items' is testing IAM policy variables such as dynamodb:LeadingKeys.

A question about protecting an API with Cognito tokens is testing the Cognito or JWT authorizer, with Lambda authorizers reserved for custom token formats, and JWT validation always includes signature, expiry, issuer and audience checks.

quiz.q: A mobile app uses an Amazon Cognito user pool for sign-in. Users must upload photos directly to Amazon S3 from the app, and each user may write only under a key prefix that matches their own identity, without the app embedding any AWS keys. What should the developer configure?
choices: An API Gateway Cognito authorizer in front of a Lambda function that receives each photo and writes it to the bucket on the user's behalf
An identity pool that trusts the user pool, with an authenticated role allowing s3:PutObject only on the user's identity ID prefix
A user pool group for all app users with a bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject for any principal that presents a valid user pool ID token
An IAM user per app user whose access keys are stored in the user pool as custom attributes and returned to the app after sign-in
quiz.explain: The identity pool exchanges the user pool token for temporary credentials, and a policy variable restricts each user to their own prefix. Choice C fails because S3 does not accept user pool ID tokens as a principal; S3 authorizes only SigV4-signed AWS credentials.

quiz.q: A team's HTTP API must accept requests only from users signed in through the company's Amazon Cognito user pool with one specific app client. The team wants no custom authorization code. What should the developer configure?
choices: A Lambda REQUEST authorizer that decodes the token payload and allows the request when the email claim ends with the company domain
IAM authorization on every route, and require the clients to sign each request with Signature Version 4 using the user pool token
A usage plan with an API key for the app client, with the key stored in the mobile app so that only the company's app can call the API
A JWT authorizer with the user pool as issuer and the app client ID as audience, attached to each route of the HTTP API
quiz.explain: An HTTP API JWT authorizer validates signature, issuer and audience with no code, so only tokens issued to that app client pass. Choice A decodes without verifying the signature, so a forged token with the right email claim would be accepted.

days.recap: User pools authenticate users and issue JWTs, identity pools turn identities into temporary AWS credentials, federation brings SAML, OIDC and social logins in, MFA and policy variables tighten access, and APIs validate tokens with Cognito, JWT or Lambda authorizers.

days.title: IAM Policies, Assumed Roles, Programmatic Access, and Presigned URLs

concepts.heading: Identity-Based and Resource-Based Policies
concepts.body: IAM decides each request by evaluating policies. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups and roles and say what that principal may do. Resource-based policies attach to a resource, such as an S3 bucket policy, an SQS queue policy, a KMS key policy or a Lambda function policy, and name the principals allowed, which can be in other accounts or AWS services. Evaluation starts from an implicit deny; an explicit Deny anywhere always wins; otherwise an Allow is needed. Within one account, an Allow in either the identity or the resource policy is enough for most services (KMS keys are the exception, because the key policy must allow access). Across accounts, both sides must allow. Permissions boundaries, SCPs and session policies only limit, never grant. Write least-privilege statements with specific actions and resource ARNs, such as dynamodb:PutItem on one table, and use IAM Access Analyzer to validate and generate policies.

concepts.heading: Assuming Roles and Temporary Credentials
concepts.body: A role has no long-term keys. A principal calls STS AssumeRole with the role ARN and a session name and receives temporary credentials: access key ID, secret access key and session token, valid from 15 minutes up to the role's maximum session duration (1 to 12 hours; role chaining is limited to 1 hour). The role's trust policy names who may assume it, and the caller also needs sts:AssumeRole permission. Cross-account access uses this two-sided handshake; third parties add an external ID condition to prevent the confused-deputy problem. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity serves OIDC tokens, for example CI/CD pipelines that federate instead of storing keys, and AssumeRoleWithSAML serves SAML. A role can require MFA through the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition, passing SerialNumber and TokenCode when assuming. Services assume their own roles: Lambda execution roles and ECS task roles. A stem about AccessDenied on AssumeRole usually means the trust policy does not list the caller.

concepts.heading: Programmatic Access and Signed Requests
concepts.body: Code and tools reach AWS with credentials that sign each request with Signature Version 4: an HMAC over the method, path, headers, payload hash, date and Region using a key derived from the secret key. The SDKs and CLI sign for you; you only sign manually for raw HTTP calls, such as an API Gateway method with IAM authorization, and then an SDK signer helps. On a developer workstation, prefer IAM Identity Center with aws configure sso and aws sso login, which writes short-lived credentials, over IAM user access keys. Named profiles in ~/.aws/config select accounts and roles: --profile dev or AWS_PROFILE=dev, and a profile with role_arn and source_profile assumes a role automatically. aws sts get-caller-identity shows which identity a call really uses. Errors such as SignatureDoesNotMatch point to a wrong secret or clock skew; ExpiredToken means temporary credentials ran out.

concepts.heading: Amazon S3 Presigned URLs
concepts.body: A presigned URL lets someone without AWS credentials perform one S3 operation, such as GET or PUT on one key, until it expires. Your backend generates it with its own credentials (generate_presigned_url in boto3, getSignedUrl in the JavaScript v3 presigner), so access is limited to what that principal may do. SigV4 presigned URLs can last up to 7 days, but a URL is valid only while the signing credentials are valid: one signed by a Lambda role session dies when that session expires, with an ExpiredToken error, whatever expiry you requested. Anything you pass while signing, such as ContentType or metadata, becomes part of the signature, so the client must send exactly the same header or receive 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch. Keep expiries short, generate the key server-side, validate the content type against an allow-list, and use presigned POST with conditions to enforce a size range.

concepts.heading: CloudFront Signed URLs and Signed Cookies
concepts.body: For private content served through CloudFront, keep the S3 bucket private with origin access control and require signatures on the cache behavior by adding a trusted key group. Your backend signs with a private key whose public key is in the key group; key groups are managed with IAM permissions and are recommended over legacy CloudFront key pairs that needed the root user. Validity depends only on the signed policy, not on any IAM session, which suits links that must last days. A signed URL protects one file, such as an installer download. Signed cookies (CloudFront-Policy, CloudFront-Signature, CloudFront-Key-Pair-Id) cover many files without changing URLs, such as all segments of a video or a members area. A canned policy has only an expiry for one exact URL; a custom policy adds a start time, an IP range and a wildcard resource such as https://d111.cloudfront.net/videos/123/*.

examPoints: A question about AccessDenied across accounts is testing that both the identity policy and the resource policy (or the role trust policy) must allow, and that an explicit Deny always wins.
A scenario about laptops, pipelines or apps holding long-term access keys is testing temporary credentials: IAM Identity Center profiles, AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and execution roles.

A question about time-limited download or upload links is testing S3 presigned URLs and their dependence on the signer's credentials, or CloudFront signed URLs and signed cookies with trusted key groups for many files and long-lived links.

quiz.q: A Lambda function generates S3 presigned GET URLs with a 3-day expiry for report downloads, using its execution role. Users report that links stop working after a few hours with an ExpiredToken error. Links must last 3 days, and long-term IAM user keys are forbidden. What should the developer do?
choices: Serve reports through CloudFront with origin access control, and issue CloudFront signed URLs with a 3-day expiry signed by a key in a trusted key group
Raise the URL expiry to 7 days, the maximum for SigV4 presigned URLs, so that links outlive the 3-day requirement with a margin
Raise the execution role's maximum session duration to 12 hours so that the credentials that sign the URLs remain valid for longer
Generate the URLs with an IAM user's access keys stored in Secrets Manager and rotated automatically every 30 days by a rotation function
quiz.explain: CloudFront signed URLs are valid for their signed policy period, independent of any IAM session, and need no IAM user. Choice B fails because a URL signed with role credentials stops working when the role session expires, whatever expiry was requested.

quiz.q: A developer's application in account A must read objects from a bucket in account B. Account B's bucket policy allows s3:GetObject for the application's role ARN, but requests still return AccessDenied. What is the most likely missing piece?
choices: A VPC gateway endpoint for S3 in account B, because cross-account requests must arrive through an endpoint owned by the bucket account
An external ID in the bucket policy, because S3 requires an external ID condition for any principal outside the bucket owner account
An identity-based policy on the role in account A that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket in account B
An S3 Access Point in account A that points to the bucket in account B, because roles can read only through local access points
quiz.explain: Cross-account access needs an Allow on both sides: the bucket policy in account B and the role's own identity policy in account A. Choice B confuses resource policies with role trust policies, where external IDs protect against the confused deputy problem.

days.recap: Know how identity and resource policies combine (explicit deny wins, cross-account needs both sides), use roles and STS for temporary credentials, sign with SigV4 through SDK profiles, and share objects with presigned URLs or CloudFront signed URLs and cookies.

days.title: Encryption with AWS KMS: At Rest, In Transit, Client-Side, and Envelope Encryption

concepts.heading: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
concepts.body: Encryption in transit protects data moving over the network with TLS: AWS service endpoints use HTTPS, and you enforce it, for example with a bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, an ALB HTTPS listener, or a database parameter that requires SSL connections. Encryption at rest protects stored data, and most AWS services integrate with AWS KMS: S3, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, CloudWatch Logs and Lambda environment variables. Choices are usually between an AWS owned key (no visibility, no cost), an AWS managed key (aws/service, visible in your account, rotated by AWS) and a customer managed key, which you control: key policy, rotation, disabling and scheduled deletion, with every use logged in CloudTrail. Requirements such as 'we must control and audit the key' or 'be able to disable access' point to a customer managed key; 'encrypt data in transit' points to TLS enforcement.

concepts.heading: S3 Server-Side Encryption Options
concepts.body: S3 encrypts every new object at rest, SSE-S3 by default, with keys that S3 manages. SSE-KMS uses a KMS key, ideally customer managed, so access needs both S3 and KMS permissions and every key use appears in CloudTrail; S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS requests and cost by using a bucket-level data key. DSSE-KMS applies two independent layers of encryption with KMS keys for workloads whose rules require dual-layer encryption. SSE-C uses a key that the client sends with every request and S3 never stores. A default encryption setting on the bucket applies when uploads do not specify one, and a bucket policy can deny PutObject requests that name the wrong method through the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption condition key. Uploads that fail with AccessDenied on an SSE-KMS bucket usually mean the role lacks kms:GenerateDataKey, and downloads that fail mean it lacks kms:Decrypt.

concepts.heading: Envelope Encryption and GenerateDataKey
concepts.body: KMS Encrypt and Decrypt work directly on at most 4 KB of data, so larger data uses envelope encryption. The application calls GenerateDataKey with a KMS key ID and receives a plaintext data key and the same key encrypted under the KMS key. It encrypts the data locally with the plaintext key (for example AES-256-GCM), removes the plaintext key from memory, and stores the encrypted data key next to the ciphertext. To decrypt, it sends the encrypted data key to KMS Decrypt, gets the plaintext key back and decrypts locally. Only the small data key ever travels to KMS, so data size does not matter and the KMS key never leaves KMS. GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext suits systems that encrypt later. An encryption context, such as {"orderId": "A-1001"}, binds additional authenticated data that must match on decrypt and appears in CloudTrail.

concepts.heading: Client-Side vs Server-Side Encryption
concepts.body: With server-side encryption, the service receives plaintext over TLS and encrypts it before storing; it is simple and transparent to code. With client-side encryption, the application encrypts before sending, so AWS stores and transfers only ciphertext, which some regulations require for the most sensitive fields. The AWS Encryption SDK implements client-side envelope encryption with KMS keyrings, includes the encrypted data keys in its message format, supports encryption context, and offers data key caching to reduce KMS calls. The Amazon S3 Encryption Client does the same for S3 objects, and the AWS Database Encryption SDK encrypts individual DynamoDB attributes. Client-side encryption prevents the service from searching or filtering on those values, so choose it only when the requirement says the provider must never see plaintext. 'Before it leaves the application' always means client-side.

concepts.heading: Key Policies, Grants, Rotation, and Quotas
concepts.body: Every KMS key has a key policy, and unlike most resources, IAM policies alone cannot grant access unless the key policy allows the account to delegate to IAM (the default policy does). So kms:Decrypt in a role's IAM policy fails if the key policy does not trust the account or the role. Grants give temporary, programmatic permissions to a principal, which AWS services use behind the scenes, for example when EBS attaches an encrypted volume. Automatic rotation of customer managed keys creates new key material on a schedule (yearly by default) while keeping old material to decrypt existing data, with no code change because the key ID stays the same. KMS has request-rate quotas per account and Region, shared across cryptographic operations; exceeding them returns ThrottlingException. Reduce calls with S3 Bucket Keys and Encryption SDK data key caching, and retry with backoff.

examPoints: A question where data must be encrypted before it leaves the application is testing client-side encryption with the AWS Encryption SDK or the S3 Encryption Client, while managed, transparent protection points to SSE-S3, SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS.
A scenario encrypting files larger than 4 KB with KMS is testing envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey, and KMS ThrottlingException is testing S3 Bucket Keys, data key caching and backoff.
A question where a role with kms:Decrypt in its IAM policy still gets AccessDenied is testing that the key policy must also allow access.

quiz.q: An application must encrypt 50 MB files with a customer managed KMS key before storing them in an on-premises archive. Calls to the KMS Encrypt API with the file content fail. What should the developer do?
choices: Request a quota increase for the maximum plaintext size of the Encrypt API so that 50 MB payloads are accepted
Split each file into 4 KB chunks and call Encrypt once per chunk, storing the encrypted chunks in order in the archive
Use GenerateDataKey, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the encrypted data key with the file
Upload the file to S3 with SSE-KMS, download the encrypted object, and store the downloaded bytes in the archive
quiz.explain: Envelope encryption encrypts any size locally with a data key, and only the small encrypted data key needs KMS to decrypt. Choice B would make thousands of KMS calls per file, run into request quotas and add cost and latency for no benefit.

quiz.q: A company stores sensitive documents in S3 and must control the key, be able to audit every use of it, and enforce that no object is uploaded without that key. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Enable default SSE-S3 encryption on the bucket, and review the S3 server access logs to audit every request to the bucket
Use SSE-C with a key stored in Secrets Manager, and require every client to send that key with each upload and download
Enable client-side encryption with a key generated by each client, and store each key as metadata on the uploaded object
Set default SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, and deny PutObject requests that do not specify SSE-KMS with that key ID
quiz.explain: A customer managed KMS key gives the company control and CloudTrail records each key use, and the bucket policy enforces the key on every upload. Choice A uses keys that S3 manages, which the company cannot control, disable or audit per use.

days.recap: Enforce TLS in transit, pick SSE-S3, SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS at rest, use client-side encryption when AWS must never see plaintext, encrypt anything over 4 KB with GenerateDataKey envelopes, and remember key policies, rotation and KMS request quotas.

days.title: Certificates and Keys for Developers: ACM, AWS Private CA, and SSH Key Pairs

concepts.heading: Public Certificates with ACM
concepts.body: AWS Certificate Manager issues public TLS certificates at no extra cost for use with integrated services, including Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon CloudFront and Amazon API Gateway custom domains. You prove control of the domain with DNS validation, a CNAME record that ACM checks, or email validation. DNS validation is preferred because ACM renews certificates automatically as long as the CNAME record stays in place, which removes expiry outages. Certificates can cover several names and wildcards such as *.example.com. ACM also imports third-party certificates with ImportCertificate, but imported certificates are not renewed by ACM, so you must reimport before expiry; CloudWatch metrics and EventBridge events for days to expiry help catch them. When a stem says a certificate is about to expire or renewal failed, check whether it was imported or whether the DNS validation record was deleted.

concepts.heading: Where Certificates Must Live
concepts.body: ACM certificates are regional resources, and each integrated service reads them from a specific Region. CloudFront distributions, and API Gateway edge-optimized custom domains, which use CloudFront, require the certificate in US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1, whatever Region the origin or API runs in. Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers with TLS listeners and API Gateway regional custom domains require the certificate in the same Region as the resource. A certificate requested in the wrong Region simply does not appear in the selection list. An ALB HTTPS listener can hold several certificates and choose one by SNI, and the listener's security policy sets the TLS versions and ciphers. For a domain served in two Regions, request a certificate in each. A stem where the certificate is missing from the CloudFront console almost always means it was requested outside us-east-1.

concepts.heading: AWS Private CA for Internal Services
concepts.body: Internal services such as microservices, IoT devices or internal APIs often need certificates for names that are not public, and they may require mutual TLS. AWS Private CA creates and operates a private certificate authority hierarchy (root and subordinate CAs) whose keys are kept in AWS-managed hardware security modules. You then request private certificates through ACM for integrated services, which ACM can renew automatically, or issue them directly through the Private CA API for workloads such as containers, devices or service meshes. Clients must trust your private root CA certificate. A CA in short-lived certificate mode issues certificates valid for at most seven days and costs less, and such short validity usually removes the need for revocation. Private CA also publishes revocation information through CRLs or OCSP. Choose Private CA when the stem mentions internal hostnames, mTLS between services, or certificates for devices; choose ACM public certificates for internet-facing endpoints.

concepts.heading: Generating Certificates for Development
concepts.body: During development you may need TLS before a real certificate exists, for example to test HTTPS locally or a test environment behind an internal hostname. A self-signed certificate can be generated with OpenSSL, for example openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 30 -subj /CN=dev.local, and imported into ACM with ImportCertificate (certificate, private key and optional chain in PEM format) so a test ALB can use it. Browsers and SDK clients will not trust it unless you add it to the local trust store, so never disable certificate verification in code to make it work; that habit leaks into production. For shared test environments, a private certificate from AWS Private CA trusted by team machines is cleaner. Keep private keys out of repositories, store them in Secrets Manager if they must be shared, and use short validity periods for development certificates.

concepts.heading: SSH Key Pairs and Keyless Access
concepts.body: EC2 Linux instances accept SSH logins with key pairs. You can let EC2 create one with aws ec2 create-key-pair, which returns the private key once, or generate your own locally with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 and upload only the public key with aws ec2 import-key-pair, so the private key never leaves your machine. The public key is placed in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys at launch, and the private key file must be readable only by you (chmod 400). EC2 Instance Connect pushes a temporary public key for one user, valid for 60 seconds, authorized by IAM, so no long-lived key needs to be distributed. Session Manager in AWS Systems Manager goes further: no inbound port 22, no SSH keys, IAM-controlled access and session logging to CloudWatch Logs or S3. A stem asking for shell access without open ports or managed keys points to Session Manager.

examPoints: A question about a certificate that cannot be selected for CloudFront or an edge-optimized API is testing that those certificates must be in us-east-1, while ALBs and regional APIs use the certificate in their own Region.

A scenario with expiring certificates is testing automatic renewal of ACM-issued certificates with DNS validation versus manual reimport of imported certificates, and internal mTLS or device certificates point to AWS Private CA.

A question about development certificates or SSH access is testing self-signed certificates imported into ACM, ssh-keygen with import-key-pair, EC2 Instance Connect, and Session Manager for keyless access.

quiz.q: A developer requested an ACM public certificate in eu-west-1 for an API Gateway edge-optimized custom domain whose API runs in eu-west-1. The certificate is issued, but it does not appear in the list when the developer creates the custom domain. What should the developer do?
choices: Wait for DNS validation to complete a second time, because edge-optimized domains require a certificate that has been renewed once
Request or import the certificate in us-east-1, because edge-optimized custom domains use CloudFront, which reads certificates from that Region
Export the certificate from ACM in eu-west-1 and upload it to API Gateway as a PEM file in the custom domain settings
Switch the certificate to email validation, because API Gateway lists only email-validated certificates for edge-optimized domains
quiz.explain: Edge-optimized custom domains are served through CloudFront, which uses ACM certificates from us-east-1 only. Choice C fails because API Gateway custom domains take an ACM certificate, and moving the files does not change the Region requirement.

quiz.q: A team's internal microservices on Amazon ECS must authenticate each other with mutual TLS using hostnames such as payments.internal. Certificates should be issued and renewed with minimal manual work, and the CA's private keys must be protected by AWS. Which service should the team use?
choices: AWS Private CA to run a private CA hierarchy and issue private certificates that the services trust through the private root
ACM public certificates validated with DNS records for payments.internal in a private hosted zone in Amazon Route 53
Self-signed certificates generated with OpenSSL in each container at startup and trusted by disabling client verification
EC2 key pairs created with ssh-keygen and imported into each task, because ECS tasks use SSH keys for service authentication
quiz.explain: AWS Private CA issues certificates for internal names and keeps CA keys in AWS-managed HSMs, and services trust the private root for mTLS. Choice B fails because public certificate authorities cannot validate or issue certificates for private names such as payments.internal.

days.recap: Use ACM public certificates with DNS validation for internet endpoints (us-east-1 for CloudFront and edge APIs), AWS Private CA for internal names and mTLS, self-signed certificates only for development, and imported public keys, Instance Connect or Session Manager for server access.

days.title: Secrets and Sensitive Data: Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, and Data Masking

concepts.heading: Secrets Manager and Rotation
concepts.body: AWS Secrets Manager stores credentials such as database passwords, API keys and OAuth client secrets, encrypted with a KMS key, and returns them with GetSecretValue. Its main differentiator is rotation: a rotation schedule invokes a Lambda rotation function that creates a new credential, sets it in the target, tests it and marks it AWSCURRENT, with the previous one kept as AWSPREVIOUS. AWS provides rotation templates for RDS, Aurora, Redshift and DocumentDB, and the single-user strategy changes one user's password, while the alternating-users strategy switches between two users to avoid a moment when a cached old password fails. RDS can also manage the master user password in Secrets Manager for you. Resource policies allow cross-account access, and secrets can be replicated to other Regions. When a stem requires automatic rotation of database credentials with no downtime, the answer is Secrets Manager rotation.

concepts.heading: Parameter Store SecureString
concepts.body: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store keeps configuration in a hierarchy such as /app/prod/db/host, with String, StringList and SecureString types; SecureString values are encrypted with a KMS key and returned decrypted when you call GetParameter with WithDecryption set to true, which also needs kms:Decrypt on that key. The standard tier is free with values up to 4 KB; the advanced tier allows 8 KB values and parameter policies such as expiration notifications, at a charge. GetParametersByPath loads a whole branch in one call. Parameter Store has no built-in rotation, so rotating a SecureString requires your own scheduled Lambda function. A common pattern is to keep non-secret configuration and feature flags in Parameter Store and credentials that must rotate in Secrets Manager, which Parameter Store can even reference. When cost matters and no rotation is needed, Parameter Store SecureString is the usual answer.

concepts.heading: Retrieving and Caching Secrets in Code
concepts.body: Fetching a secret on every request adds latency and cost and can hit API rate limits, so cache it. In Lambda, read it once during initialization or keep it in a module-level variable with a short TTL, use the AWS Secrets Manager caching libraries, or add the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, which caches parameters and secrets and serves them to the function over a local HTTP endpoint. When rotation happens, a cached credential can become stale, so on an authentication failure the code should refresh the secret and retry once; the alternating-users rotation strategy reduces the risk further. Infrastructure templates should use dynamic references such as {{resolve:secretsmanager:prod/db:SecretString:password}} instead of literal passwords. Never place secrets in environment variables as plain text, in code or in container images, and scan commits for them. 'Reduce GetSecretValue calls' points to caching or the extension.

concepts.heading: Masking PII and PHI in Logs
concepts.body: Logs often outlive the data they describe and are read by more people, so personal and health data must not appear in them. First, fix the code: log identifiers such as a customer ID or a request ID, not names, card numbers or full request bodies. As a safety net, attach a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy to a log group or the whole account. It uses managed data identifiers, such as credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, email addresses, AWS secret keys and health identifiers, plus custom identifiers to find sensitive values when events are ingested. Matches are masked at every read path, including the console, GetLogEvents, Logs Insights, metric filters and subscription filters, and only principals with logs:Unmask can see the original values. Audit findings can go to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose. Events ingested before the policy existed are not masked.

concepts.heading: Limiting Access to Sensitive Data
concepts.body: Masking is one layer; access control is the other. Grant only the principals that need sensitive data access to it, for example a role with dynamodb:GetItem on one table and a dynamodb:Attributes condition that returns only non-sensitive attributes to most callers, or separate tables for sensitive fields. Encrypt sensitive stores with customer managed KMS keys so the key policy becomes a second gate: a CloudWatch Logs group encrypted with a symmetric customer managed key requires kms:Decrypt as well as Logs permissions, and disabling the key makes the data unreadable. Tag resources by data classification and use attribute-based access control conditions on those tags. Return generic errors to clients and keep stack traces in logs. Use IAM Access Analyzer to find unused permissions and public or cross-account access. A stem asking that only one team see raw values points to logs:Unmask or a dedicated KMS key policy.

examPoints: A question requiring automatic credential rotation is testing Secrets Manager, while cheap storage of encrypted configuration without rotation is testing Parameter Store SecureString with WithDecryption and kms:Decrypt.

A scenario with too many secret retrievals, stale credentials after rotation, or passwords in templates is testing caching libraries, the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, refresh-on-failure and dynamic references.

A question about PII or PHI in logs is testing CloudWatch Logs data protection policies with managed data identifiers and logs:Unmask, plus least-privilege and customer managed KMS keys as a second gate.

quiz.q: Application logs in a CloudWatch Logs log group sometimes contain customer email addresses and credit card numbers. Developers query the group with Logs Insights and must not see these values, while the security team must be able to see them during investigations. What should the developer configure?
choices: A metric filter that counts log events matching card number patterns, with an alarm that notifies the developers whenever a match occurs
A subscription filter that sends events to a Lambda function, which removes sensitive values and writes the events to a second log group
A data protection policy with managed data identifiers on the log group, and logs:Unmask granted only to the security team's role
A shorter retention period of one day on the log group so that the sensitive values are deleted before most developers query them
quiz.explain: A data protection policy masks matches at ingestion for every reader, including Logs Insights, and logs:Unmask controls who sees raw values. Choice B leaves the unmasked originals in the first log group and adds custom code that must be maintained and secured.

quiz.q: A Lambda function reads an RDS password from Secrets Manager on every invocation. At peak traffic, GetSecretValue calls add latency and cost, and the password rotates every 30 days with the single-user strategy. What should the developer do?
choices: Copy the password into an environment variable at deployment time and redeploy the function after each rotation
Store the password as a SecureString in Parameter Store, because GetParameter calls have no latency or request quotas
Disable rotation on the secret so that the password can be cached in the function for the lifetime of each environment
Cache the secret with the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension or a caching library, and refresh it when a login fails
quiz.explain: Caching removes most GetSecretValue calls, and refreshing on an authentication failure handles a rotated password. Choice A puts the secret in plain configuration and breaks every time the password rotates until someone redeploys.

days.recap: Rotate credentials with Secrets Manager, keep cheap encrypted configuration in Parameter Store, cache secrets and refresh on failure, mask PII and PHI in logs with data protection policies and logs:Unmask, and gate sensitive data with least privilege and customer managed keys.

days.title: Using AI Services Safely: Model Access, Private Connectivity, Data Privacy, and Logs

concepts.heading: Requesting and Managing Model Access
concepts.body: Access to many serverless foundation models on Amazon Bedrock is enabled by default, so there is no per-model request queue for them. For a third-party model, the first invocation in an account starts an AWS Marketplace subscription in the background; the calling principal needs aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions, and the account needs a valid payment method. Anthropic models also need a one-time first-time-use form. If a prerequisite is missing, a few calls may succeed during setup and then every call returns AccessDeniedException. Because access is on by default, organizations that must review a model's license first block it with an SCP or IAM deny and lift the deny after approval. Day-to-day access is then plain IAM: allow bedrock:InvokeModel and, for streaming, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on specific model or inference profile ARNs, and allow the profile plus the model in every destination Region for cross-Region inference.

concepts.heading: Credentials for Bedrock: Roles and API Keys
concepts.body: Applications should call Bedrock with role credentials and SigV4, like any AWS API. For HTTP clients that only accept a bearer token, Bedrock API keys exist in two kinds. A short-term key is generated from an existing principal's credentials, for example with the aws-bedrock-token-generator library; it inherits that principal's permissions, works only in the Region where it was generated, and lasts up to 12 hours or the remaining session time. Generating one is cheap, so a service can create a new one per request from its task role. A long-term key is an IAM service-specific credential tied to an IAM user and is intended for exploration only. To revoke a leaked long-term key, deactivate or delete the service-specific credential; a short-term key cannot be deleted, so deny bedrock:CallWithBearerToken and bedrock-mantle:CallWithBearerToken for that identity or invalidate the session that generated it.

concepts.heading: Private Connectivity with VPC Endpoints
concepts.body: To keep prompts off the public internet, call Bedrock through interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). Bedrock splits its APIs across endpoints: bedrock for the control plane, bedrock-runtime for inference (InvokeModel, Converse, ApplyGuardrail), bedrock-agent and bedrock-agent-runtime for Knowledge Bases, and bedrock-mantle for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint. A Lambda function in private subnets with no NAT gateway needs an interface endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS enabled, so the SDK resolves the normal hostname without code changes, and the endpoint's security group must allow HTTPS from the function. There is no gateway endpoint for Bedrock. A custom endpoint policy then limits what passes through: for example, allow bedrock:InvokeModel only for the application role on one approved inference profile and its models, which blocks credentials brought in from other accounts, something an identity policy alone cannot do.

concepts.heading: Data Privacy: Training, Providers, and Residency
concepts.body: Developers must be able to answer where prompts go. Amazon Bedrock does not use your prompts and completions to train AWS models or share them with model providers. Each provider's model runs in a model deployment account owned and operated by the Bedrock service team; providers have no access to those accounts, so they cannot see prompts, completions or logs. Data in transit uses TLS 1.2 or later. Model invocation logging is off by default and, when enabled, writes only to your own CloudWatch Logs group or S3 bucket in the same account and Region. Residency is controlled with inference choices and IAM: a geographic inference profile such as us. keeps requests inside one geography, while a global profile can route worldwide. To block global routing permanently, add an explicit Deny on bedrock:InvokeModel* where aws:RequestedRegion equals unspecified, because a list of Region names never matches the global evaluation.

concepts.heading: Protecting Sensitive Content in Invocation Logs
concepts.body: Model invocation logs contain full request and response bodies, so they hold whatever users typed. Configure delivery deliberately: for CloudWatch Logs, Bedrock uses an IAM role that trusts bedrock.amazonaws.com; for S3, the bucket policy and, with SSE-KMS, the key policy must allow the bedrock.amazonaws.com service principal with aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn conditions. Then protect the content. Attach a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy so card numbers, Social Security numbers and other identifiers are masked for every reader, with logs:Unmask only for the team that needs raw values. Encrypt the log group with a symmetric customer managed KMS key and grant kms:Decrypt only to approved readers, so broad Logs read permissions are not enough and disabling the key makes the data unreadable. To trace end users, put a pseudonymous ID in Converse requestMetadata, never an email address in prompts, tags or names.

examPoints: A question where Bedrock calls succeed briefly and then fail with AccessDeniedException on a third-party model is testing automatic model access through AWS Marketplace subscriptions and the aws-marketplace permissions.

A scenario requiring prompts to stay off the internet or limiting which principals and models can be used from a VPC is testing an interface endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS and a custom endpoint policy.

A question about who can see prompts is testing that providers cannot access Bedrock's model deployment accounts, that inputs are not used for training, and that invocation logs need data protection policies, KMS keys and pseudonymous requestMetadata.

quiz.q: A Lambda function in private subnets with no NAT gateway must call the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. Compliance requires that prompts never use a public network path, and the developer does not want to change the SDK client configuration. What should the developer configure?
choices: A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon Bedrock in the private subnets' route tables, with an endpoint policy that allows bedrock:InvokeModel
An interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.region.bedrock, because that endpoint serves both the control plane and the runtime inference APIs
A NAT gateway in a public subnet and a security group on the function that allows outbound HTTPS only to the Bedrock IP address ranges
An interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.region.bedrock-runtime with private DNS enabled, and HTTPS allowed from the function's security group
quiz.explain: Converse is a runtime API served by the bedrock-runtime endpoint, and private DNS lets the unchanged SDK resolve the normal hostname to the endpoint. Choice B fails because the bedrock endpoint serves only control plane APIs, so Converse calls would still have no route.

quiz.q: Bedrock model invocation logs are delivered to a CloudWatch Logs log group. The support team needs to identify which end user made each call, but users' email addresses must not appear in the logs. All calls come from one Lambda execution role. What should the developer do?
choices: Put a pseudonymous user ID in the requestMetadata of each Converse call and keep the mapping to the email address in the application database
Rely on the identity.arn field of each log record, because Bedrock records the end user who started the Lambda invocation
Add the user's email address to the system prompt of each call so that it appears in the logged request body next to the message
Create one inference profile per user tagged with the user's email address, and call Converse with that profile as the modelId
quiz.explain: requestMetadata values are written to each log record and can be filtered, and an opaque ID keeps personal data out of the logs. Choice B fails because identity.arn is the signing principal, which is the same Lambda role for every user.

days.recap: Model access is on by default through Marketplace subscriptions and controlled with IAM or SCP denies, Bedrock API keys should be short-term, private calls use bedrock-runtime interface endpoints with endpoint policies, providers never see your data, and invocation logs need masking, KMS and pseudonymous IDs.

days.title: Guardrails and Agent Security: Filtering Inputs and Outputs, Tool Authorization, and Human Approval

concepts.heading: Guardrail Policies
concepts.body: An Amazon Bedrock guardrail is a reusable set of policies that evaluates both user inputs and model outputs. Content filters detect categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence and misconduct, each with a strength setting. The prompt attack filter detects jailbreaks, prompt injection and prompt leakage in user input. Denied topics are described in natural language with sample phrases, for example 'investment advice', and block matching requests or answers. Word filters block custom words and profanity. Sensitive information filters detect PII types such as email, phone number or card number, plus custom regular expressions, and either block the content or mask it by replacing values with placeholders such as {EMAIL}. Contextual grounding checks flag answers that are not supported by the provided source or not relevant to the query. You test a working draft, publish numbered versions, and can encrypt the guardrail with a customer managed key via kmsKeyId.

concepts.heading: Applying Guardrails in Code
concepts.body: A guardrail is applied per request, not attached to a model or role. With Converse and ConverseStream, pass guardrailConfig with guardrailIdentifier, guardrailVersion and optionally trace set to enabled; when the guardrail intervenes, stopReason is guardrail_intervened and the output contains the configured blocked message. With InvokeModel, use the X-Amzn-Bedrock-GuardrailIdentifier and GuardrailVersion headers, and wrap user text in amazon-bedrock-guardrails-guardContent tags with a new random tagSuffix per request, because prompt attacks in untagged InvokeModel input are not filtered; Converse uses guardContent blocks instead. ApplyGuardrail evaluates any text without invoking a model, with source INPUT before a call and OUTPUT after, so the same guardrail can protect a self-hosted model or a model outside Bedrock. To require a guardrail, add an explicit IAM Deny on the inference actions when bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier is not the approved ARN and version.

concepts.heading: What Guardrails Do Not See
concepts.body: Guardrails in guardrailConfig evaluate message text, model text responses and guardContent blocks, but not tool use fields: the arguments the model generates for a tool (toolUse.input), the tool results your application returns, and the tool definitions themselves. So a sensitive information filter can mask email addresses in chat replies while a create_ticket tool still writes raw emails to a database. The fix is in your code: validate tool arguments against the schema and business rules, and pass any free text through ApplyGuardrail before acting on it or storing it. Model-generated code is another blind spot. Running it with exec() inside your function gives it the function's IAM role and network access; instead, run it in an isolated sandbox such as AgentCore Code Interpreter with the SANDBOX network mode and a least-privilege execution role, for example s3:GetObject on one upload prefix only.

concepts.heading: Tool-Use Authorization and Session Isolation
concepts.body: Agents act through tools, so each tool call must be authorized as the right identity with the least privilege. AgentCore Identity lets an agent call third-party APIs with a user's own permissions: an OAuth credential provider using the authorization code (user federation) flow stores the user's tokens in a token vault, and the tool requests a token for that user, so the agent code never holds long-lived secrets. The client credentials flow, by contrast, acts as the app with the app's own scopes. AgentCore Gateway exposes APIs as MCP tools with separate inbound authorization (IAM or a JWT authorizer with allowed clients and audiences) controlling who may list and call tools, and outbound authorization for calls to targets. In AgentCore Runtime, give each user conversation its own unique runtimeSessionId; each session runs in its own isolated environment, and a shared hardcoded ID leaks one user's context into another's.

concepts.heading: Human-in-the-Loop Approval for Sensitive Actions
concepts.body: Some agent actions, such as issuing refunds, deleting records or sending money, must never run on the model's decision alone. In Converse tool use the model only proposes a call with stopReason tool_use; your application executes tools, so it can pause before a sensitive tool, ask a human, and run the tool only after approval, returning a toolResult with status error or a denial message if rejected so the model can explain it to the user. For longer approvals, a Step Functions workflow can use a task with .waitForTaskToken: it sends the token to a reviewer through SNS or a ticket, waits, and continues only when SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure is called with that token. A system prompt telling the model to ask for approval is not a control, because prompt injection can talk the model out of it. Log every approval decision for audit.

examPoints: A question about blocking harmful content, denied subjects, jailbreaks or PII in model input and output is testing guardrail policies, guardrailConfig on Converse with stopReason guardrail_intervened, input tags for InvokeModel, and ApplyGuardrail for non-Bedrock models.
A scenario where PII still reaches a database through an agent's tool is testing that guardrails skip tool arguments and results, so the application must screen them, for example with ApplyGuardrail.

A question about agents acting for users, shared conversations or refunds without approval is testing AgentCore Identity user-delegated OAuth, unique runtime session IDs, gateway inbound authorization, and application-enforced human approval.

quiz.q: A developer calls InvokeModel with guardrail identifier and version headers. The guardrail's prompt attack filter is set to High, but jailbreak text typed by users still reaches the model. The request body contains the developer's system instructions followed by the raw user text in one prompt string. What should the developer do?
choices: Set the guardrail version header to DRAFT, because the prompt attack filter runs only on the working draft of a guardrail
Wrap only the user text in guardContent input tags and send a new random tagSuffix in the guardrail configuration on every request
Move the system instructions into a denied topic so that the guardrail evaluates only the remaining user text in the prompt string
Raise the prompt attack filter strength for model responses so that injected instructions are caught when the model repeats them
quiz.explain: With InvokeModel, the prompt attack filter evaluates only text marked as user input with input tags, and a random suffix per request stops users from forging a closing tag. Choice A fails because published versions and the draft run the same filters, so changing the version does not tag the user input.

quiz.q: A customer-service agent uses Converse tool use. One tool issues refunds. The security team requires that no refund is ever issued without a human's explicit approval, even if a user tries prompt injection. How should the developer implement this?
choices: Add a system prompt instruction that the model must always ask the user for confirmation before it calls the refund tool
Attach a guardrail with a denied topic for refunds, so that any model response that mentions a refund is blocked and logged
Give the refund tool a description that says it requires approval, so that the model requests the tool only after approval
On a toolUse for the refund tool, pause and run it only after a human approves, otherwise return a denied toolResult
quiz.explain: The application, not the model, executes tools, so gating the call on human approval is deterministic and cannot be bypassed by prompt text. Choice A depends on the model obeying an instruction, which prompt injection can defeat.

days.recap: Guardrails filter content, prompt attacks, denied topics, words and PII on inputs and outputs, applied per request or through ApplyGuardrail and enforceable with IAM; tool arguments, generated code and sensitive actions still need application-side screening, sandboxing, per-user identity, isolated sessions and human approval.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Security

concepts.heading: Authentication and Authorization Recap
concepts.body: Domain 2 separates who a caller is from what it may do. Cognito user pools sign users in, federate SAML, OIDC and social identities, enforce MFA and issue JWTs; identity pools exchange those identities for temporary AWS credentials, with policy variables such as dynamodb:LeadingKeys limiting each user to their own data. APIs validate tokens with Cognito or JWT authorizers, or Lambda authorizers for custom formats, and every JWT check includes signature, expiry, issuer and audience. IAM evaluation starts at implicit deny, an explicit Deny always wins, and cross-account access needs both the identity and the resource side. Roles and STS replace long-term keys everywhere: execution roles, AssumeRole with trust policies and external IDs, web identity federation for pipelines, and IAM Identity Center profiles on laptops. Sort a stem into user identity or AWS identity first, and half the choices fall away.

concepts.heading: Time-Limited Access Recap
concepts.body: Several tools grant temporary access without sharing credentials. S3 presigned URLs give one operation on one object; they last up to 7 days with SigV4 but never longer than the credentials that signed them, and signed headers such as ContentType must match exactly. CloudFront signed URLs protect single files and signed cookies protect many files without changing URLs, both signed by a key in a trusted key group, with custom policies for wildcards, start times and IP ranges, and validity independent of IAM sessions. STS credentials last from 15 minutes up to the role's maximum session, and short-term Bedrock API keys last up to 12 hours. Common traps: a presigned URL dying early because a role signed it, a 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch from a different Content-Type, and a canned policy that cannot cover video segments.

concepts.heading: Encryption and Certificates Recap
concepts.body: Encrypt in transit with TLS and policies such as aws:SecureTransport, and at rest with KMS-integrated services. In S3, SSE-S3 is the default, SSE-KMS adds key control and CloudTrail auditing (with Bucket Keys to cut KMS calls), DSSE-KMS adds a second layer, and SSE-C uses client-supplied keys. Client-side encryption with the AWS Encryption SDK keeps plaintext inside the application. KMS Encrypt handles at most 4 KB, so larger data uses envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey. Key policies must allow access even when IAM does, rotation keeps the same key ID, and KMS quotas cause ThrottlingException. For certificates, ACM issues and renews public certificates with DNS validation, CloudFront and edge-optimized APIs read them from us-east-1, AWS Private CA covers internal names and mTLS, and developers use self-signed certificates, imported SSH public keys, Instance Connect or Session Manager.

concepts.heading: Secrets and Sensitive Data Recap
concepts.body: Secrets Manager stores credentials and rotates them with Lambda rotation functions, including managed templates for RDS and alternating-users rotation; Parameter Store SecureString is cheaper encrypted configuration without built-in rotation, read with WithDecryption and kms:Decrypt. Cache secrets with the caching libraries or the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, refresh after an authentication failure, and reference secrets in templates with dynamic references rather than literals. For PII and PHI, log identifiers instead of personal data, attach CloudWatch Logs data protection policies with managed data identifiers so values are masked on every read path, grant logs:Unmask narrowly, and encrypt sensitive log groups with customer managed keys whose policies form a second gate. IAM Access Analyzer and least-privilege conditions keep access to sensitive stores small and reviewable.

concepts.heading: AI Security Recap
concepts.body: The new task 2.3 asks how to use AI services safely. Model access is on by default through AWS Marketplace subscriptions, controlled with IAM and SCP denies, and invoked with specific bedrock:InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream permissions; Bedrock API keys should be short-term. Interface endpoints for bedrock-runtime with private DNS keep prompts off the internet, and endpoint policies block foreign credentials. Bedrock does not train on your prompts, providers cannot reach the model deployment accounts, and residency is enforced with geographic profiles and a Deny on aws:RequestedRegion unspecified. Invocation logs need data protection policies, KMS keys and pseudonymous requestMetadata. Guardrails filter content, prompt attacks, denied topics, words and PII, but not tool arguments, so applications screen tool inputs, sandbox generated code, use AgentCore Identity and unique session IDs, and require human approval for sensitive actions.

examPoints: A Domain 2 question almost always asks one of four things: who is the caller, what may it do, how is the data protected at rest, in transit and in logs, or how is a secret, certificate or AI interaction kept safe; classify the stem before reading the choices.

A question offering a prompt instruction, a longer expiry, or an IAM user's keys as the security fix is usually testing that deterministic controls (explicit denies, endpoint policies, application-enforced approval, temporary credentials) beat convenience.

quiz.q: A platform team requires that every Converse and InvokeModel call made by an application role uses guardrail gr-7 at version 3, and calls with no guardrail or another guardrail must fail, even if developers later add broader Bedrock permissions to the role. What should the developer do?
choices: Configure account-level guardrail enforcement for gr-7 version 3 so that Bedrock rejects any call whose request names no guardrail
Add a statement that allows bedrock:InvokeModel only when a request tag named guardrail equals gr-7:3, and tag every request
Add an explicit Deny on the inference actions when bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier is not the gr-7:3 ARN, and allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail
Create an AWS Config rule that inspects CloudTrail InvokeModel events and revokes the role's sessions when a guardrail is missing
quiz.explain: An explicit Deny conditioned on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier makes any other call fail, and no later Allow can override it. Choice A applies an extra guardrail to all calls in the account but does not reject requests, and it is not scoped to one role.

quiz.q: A web app lets signed-in users download their monthly statements, which are stored in a private S3 bucket encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key. The backend Lambda function generates presigned GET URLs, but users receive AccessDenied when they open them. The function's role allows s3:GetObject on the bucket. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Make the bucket public for the statements prefix, because presigned URLs cannot be used with buckets that block public access
Allow the function's role kms:Decrypt on the customer managed key, in both its IAM policy and the key policy if required
Switch the presigned URLs to Signature Version 2, because SSE-KMS objects can be downloaded only with SigV2 presigned URLs
Generate the URLs with the users' Cognito ID tokens instead of the role credentials, so that S3 authorizes each user directly
quiz.explain: A presigned URL carries the signer's permissions, and reading an SSE-KMS object also requires kms:Decrypt on the key. Choice A is never needed, because presigned URLs work with private buckets that block public access.

days.recap: Domain 2 rewards precise controls: verified identities and temporary credentials, least-privilege policies where explicit denies win, the right encryption and certificate in the right place, rotated and masked secrets, and AI interactions protected by private endpoints, guardrails, scoped tools and human approval.

days.title: Deployment Artifacts: Dependencies, Dockerfiles, Amazon ECR and Code Repositories

concepts.heading: Managing Dependencies Inside a Package
concepts.body: A deployable artifact should contain everything the code needs to run and nothing that changes per environment. Libraries are resolved at build time from a lock file (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, pom.xml with pinned versions) so that every build of the same commit produces the same dependency tree, and they are bundled into the .zip, the layer or the container image. Values that differ between dev, test and prod, such as a table name, an API URL or a log level, stay outside the package and arrive as environment variables or from a configuration service at run time; that is how one artifact can be built once and promoted through every environment. Configuration files that ship inside the package hold only defaults. AWS CodeArtifact can serve internal and public npm, PyPI or Maven packages from one private endpoint. On the exam, an answer that rebuilds per environment or bakes secrets into the image is usually wrong.

concepts.heading: Dockerfiles, Layers and Multi-Stage Builds
concepts.body: Every RUN, COPY or ADD instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer, and two rules follow. Layers only add, so a later RUN rm -rf does not shrink an image whose earlier layer wrote 400 MB. Cache reuse stops at the first changed instruction, so slow and rarely changing steps go first: copy only the dependency manifest (pom.xml, package.json, requirements.txt), download dependencies, and only then copy the source. A multi-stage build has several FROM lines, and only the last stage becomes the pushed image. For example, a build stage FROM a Maven and JDK image runs mvn package, and a final stage FROM a JRE-only image copies just the JAR with COPY --from=build. The result is smaller, builds faster after source-only edits and ships no compiler or source code. Questions about large images or slow rebuilds after every code change point to dependency-first ordering and multi-stage builds.

concepts.heading: Image Tags, Digests and Tag Immutability
concepts.body: A tag such as orders:stable is a movable pointer; the digest (sha256:...) identifies exact image content and never changes. A common scheme tags each build with the Git commit SHA and adds environment tags such as staging when an image is promoted. With the repository setting IMMUTABLE, Amazon ECR rejects any push that would repoint an existing tag with ImageTagAlreadyExistsException, which protects release tags. When a few tags must keep moving, use IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION with a wildcard filter such as staging, so every other tag stays fixed. To promote the exact tested bytes, retag without Docker: aws ecr batch-get-image fetches the manifest of build-512 and aws ecr put-image writes it again under prod-2026.11.03, so both tags share one digest. Rebuilding from the same commit is not a promotion, because base images or unpinned dependencies can change the digest.

concepts.heading: Pushing Images from CodeBuild and Multi-Architecture Tags
concepts.body: Docker does not understand IAM, so a build must first log in to the registry. In the buildspec pre_build phase, aws ecr get-login-password calls ecr:GetAuthorizationToken with the CodeBuild service role and pipes a token, valid for 12 hours, into docker login --username AWS --password-stdin for the registry URI. Without that step docker push fails with no basic auth credentials. The service role also needs the layer upload actions (ecr:InitiateLayerUpload, ecr:UploadLayerPart, ecr:CompleteLayerUpload, ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability) and ecr:PutImage on the repository; long-term access keys in environment variables are never the answer. When one tag must run on both x86_64 and Graviton hosts, build an amd64 and an arm64 image and push a manifest list that references both; the runtime picks the matching entry. An exec format error after switching an ECS task to ARM64 means the image was built for the other architecture.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle Policies and Image Scanning
concepts.body: An ECR lifecycle policy is a list of rules, each with a rulePriority, a selection (tagStatus untagged, tagged with a tagPatternList or tagPrefixList, or any) and a count type: imageCountMoreThan keeps the newest N, sinceImagePushed acts on images older than N days. The action is expire (or transition to archive); there is no retain action, and any image no rule selects is kept, so release images are protected simply by never selecting them. For example, rule 1 expires untagged images 3 days after push and rule 2 keeps the 20 newest dev-* images. Scanning is set at the registry level. Basic scanning checks operating system packages on push or on demand. Enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector, covers programming language packages such as pip and npm too, and with continuous scan re-evaluates images when new CVEs are published; route its findings with an EventBridge rule to SNS.

concepts.heading: Using Code Repositories in Deployment Environments
concepts.body: The repository is the source of truth for both application code and infrastructure templates, and deployment environments read from it rather than from a developer's laptop. AWS CodePipeline connects to GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket through a connection (AWS CodeConnections) and can also use AWS CodeCommit, an S3 object or an ECR image as its source. A push to a watched branch starts the pipeline, and the source action passes the exact commit to CodeBuild as an artifact, so CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION can become the image tag. Because the commit ID travels with the artifact, any running version can be traced back to the code that produced it. Build tooling, buildspec.yml, Dockerfile and IaC templates all live in the same repository, reviewed through pull requests. Exam scenarios that copy code by hand to servers or build from a workstation are pointing you toward a repository-driven pipeline instead.

examPoints: A question that requires commit-SHA tags never to be overwritten while a staging or latest tag keeps moving is testing ECR tag immutability with an exclusion filter (IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION), not a return to MUTABLE.
A question about promoting the exact image that passed testing is testing retagging by digest (batch-get-image plus put-image) instead of rebuilding from the same commit.
A question that asks for alerts on language-package CVEs in images already stored in ECR is testing enhanced scanning with continuous scan through Amazon Inspector and an EventBridge rule.

quiz.q: An ECR repository holds images tagged with Git commit SHAs, and the pipeline also moves a staging tag to the image currently in staging. After the security team set the repository to IMMUTABLE, pushing the staging tag fails with ImageTagAlreadyExistsException. SHA tags must never be overwritten. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Switch the repository back to MUTABLE and rely on commit SHAs being unique so that no pipeline run ever pushes the same SHA tag twice
Keep IMMUTABLE and add a lifecycle rule that expires images tagged staging one day after push so the old tag is gone before the next push
Set the repository to IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION with a wildcard exclusion filter for staging so only that tag can be repointed
Keep IMMUTABLE and push the staging tag with a client-side force option so that Docker overrides the registry setting for that one tag
quiz.explain: IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION keeps every tag immutable except those matching the exclusion filter, so SHA tags stay protected and staging can move. Choice B fails because an expire action deletes the whole image, including its SHA tag, and lifecycle rules run asynchronously rather than at push time.

quiz.q: A team uses ECR basic scanning on push for Python services. A critical CVE was published today for a pip library inside images pushed last week that are still running, and nobody was alerted. The team wants automatic findings for OS and language packages, re-evaluated when new CVEs appear, with a notification to an SNS topic. What should the developer configure?
choices: Enable enhanced scanning with continuous scan on the registry and add an EventBridge rule for Amazon Inspector findings that targets the SNS topic
Keep basic scanning and add a scheduled Lambda function that calls StartImageScan for every image daily and publishes any findings to the SNS topic
Keep basic scanning and change the registry scan-on-push filter to a wildcard so every repository is scanned, then email the results to the team
Sign every image with AWS Signer and add an ECS policy that blocks unsigned images so images with known CVEs cannot be deployed at all
quiz.explain: Enhanced scanning through Amazon Inspector covers language packages such as pip and, with continuous scan, updates findings when new CVEs are published; Inspector findings reach SNS through EventBridge. Choice B still uses basic scanning, which only checks operating system packages, so the pip library would never be reported.

days.recap: Build each artifact once with pinned dependencies and no environment-specific values, use dependency-first multi-stage Dockerfiles, tag by commit SHA with immutability (plus exclusions for moving tags), and let lifecycle policies, enhanced scanning and a repository-driven pipeline keep ECR clean and safe.

days.title: Environment Configuration: AppConfig, Parameter Store, API Gateway Stages, Lambda Aliases, Amplify and Copilot

concepts.heading: Environment-Specific Values in Parameter Store and Secrets Manager
concepts.body: Keeping configuration out of the artifact means it must live somewhere each environment can read. Systems Manager Parameter Store organizes values in hierarchies such as /orders/dev/table-name and /orders/prod/table-name, so code reads its own environment's branch with GetParametersByPath, and IAM policies can restrict a prod role to /orders/prod/*. Plain values use String, sensitive ones SecureString encrypted with KMS. Database passwords and API keys that need automatic rotation belong in Secrets Manager, again one secret per environment. Lambda environment variables are fine for non-secret values such as STAGE=prod or the parameter path, and CloudFormation can inject values at deploy time with dynamic references such as {{resolve:ssm:/orders/prod/table-name}}. Cache what you read, because fetching on every invocation adds latency and API calls. The exam signal: one artifact plus per-environment parameters, never a separate build for each environment.

concepts.heading: AWS AppConfig for Feature Flags and Safe Configuration Changes
concepts.body: AWS AppConfig deploys configuration the way CodeDeploy deploys code. An application has environments (dev, prod) and configuration profiles, either feature flags or freeform JSON or YAML stored in AppConfig, Parameter Store or S3. Validators, a JSON Schema or a Lambda function, reject a bad configuration before it is deployed. A deployment strategy controls the rollout, for example the AWS-recommended AppConfig.Linear20PercentEvery6Minutes, followed by a bake time, and CloudWatch alarms attached to the environment make AppConfig roll the configuration back if they fire. Lambda functions read configuration through the AppConfig Agent Lambda extension, which retrieves and caches it locally so the handler calls a localhost endpoint instead of the AppConfig API on every invocation. Choose AppConfig when a scenario wants to turn a feature on for some users, change behavior without redeploying code, validate the change, or roll a configuration change back automatically.

concepts.heading: API Gateway Stages, Stage URLs and Endpoints
concepts.body: A deployment of a REST API is a snapshot, and a stage (dev, qa, prod) is a named reference to a deployment with its own settings: throttling, caching, logging, an optional canary, and stage variables. Each stage has its own invoke URL, https://{api-id}.execute-api.{region}.amazonaws.com/{stage}, so testers call /qa while customers call /prod. Changes to resources or methods reach a stage only after you deploy the API to that stage. HTTP APIs offer a $default stage with automatic deployment. The endpoint type decides where the API is reachable: edge-optimized (through CloudFront points of presence), Regional (clients in the same Region or your own CDN) or private (only from a VPC through an interface endpoint). A custom domain name such as api.example.com with base path mappings hides the stage from clients, for example mapping /v1 to the prod stage. Exam questions about separate URLs per environment or a stable public hostname are testing stages and custom domains.

concepts.heading: Lambda Versions and Aliases as Environments
concepts.body: Publishing a Lambda version freezes its code and configuration under a number; $LATEST stays editable. An alias such as dev, qa or prod is a named pointer to one version, so promoting a release means moving the alias, and rolling back means moving it back. An alias can also split traffic, for example 90 percent to version 6 and 10 percent to version 7, which is what CodeDeploy uses for canary deployments. API Gateway selects the alias through a stage variable: the integration ARN ends in :${stageVariables.lambdaAlias}, and each stage sets lambdaAlias. Because every qualified ARN has its own resource-based policy, you must run aws lambda add-permission with --qualifier for each alias, otherwise the stage returns HTTP 500 and the execution log says Invalid permissions on Lambda function. Event sources and other callers should also point at the alias ARN, not at $LATEST.

concepts.heading: Container Image Tags and AWS Copilot Environments
concepts.body: For containers, the environment is selected by the image tag or digest a task definition or pod spec references and by the cluster and account it runs in. A pipeline builds orders:3f2a9c1 once, deploys it to staging, then adds a prod tag or a new task definition revision that references the same digest. Unique tags per build make deployments explicit and easy to roll back. AWS Copilot is a command line tool that creates ECS and Fargate applications with named environments: copilot app init, copilot env init --name test, then copilot svc deploy --env test. Each environment gets its own networking, cluster and service stacks, and per-environment overrides live in the service manifest. The Copilot CLI reached end of support on June 12, 2026 (no updates or security fixes; existing stacks keep running), so new projects use CDK, SAM or CloudFormation, but the exam guide still names Copilot environments: a separate, repeatable stack per stage from one manifest.

concepts.heading: AWS Amplify Branch Environments
concepts.body: AWS Amplify Hosting connects a Git repository and builds and deploys each connected branch separately, so main can be production and develop can be staging, each with its own URL. Branch auto-detection can connect new feature branches automatically, and pull request previews give reviewers a temporary deployment for each pull request. Environment variables are set once at the app level and apply to every branch, including those connected later; a branch override gives one branch a different value. For example, API_URL is the staging API for all branches, and main overrides it with the production API, so each value is defined exactly once. For a single-page app these values are compiled into the JavaScript bundle at build time and are visible to users, so they must never hold secrets. Creating a second Amplify app for production works but duplicates settings, which is usually the wrong answer.

examPoints: A question where a new API Gateway stage that calls a Lambda alias through a stage variable returns HTTP 500 with Invalid permissions on Lambda function is testing the per-alias resource-based permission (lambda add-permission with a qualifier).
A question that wants to change application behavior or flip a feature flag without redeploying code, with validation and automatic rollback on alarms, is testing AWS AppConfig deployment strategies.
A question about giving one Amplify branch a different build value with the least duplicated configuration is testing app-level environment variables with branch overrides.
