quiz.q: A REST API integrates with arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:orders:${stageVariables.lambdaAlias}. The dev stage works. A new qa stage with lambdaAlias set to qa returns HTTP 500, and the execution log shows Invalid permissions on Lambda function. The qa alias exists and points to version 7. What should the developer do?
choices: Add lambda:InvokeFunction for the orders function to the function's execution role so that the function may be invoked through the qa alias
Redeploy the API to the qa stage, because stage variable values are only read when a new deployment of the API is created
Point the qa alias at $LATEST instead of version 7, because API Gateway can invoke an alias only when it targets the unpublished version
Add a resource-based permission on the orders function qualified with the qa alias that allows apigateway.amazonaws.com to invoke it
quiz.explain: Each alias is a separate qualified ARN with its own resource-based policy, so the qa alias needs its own add-permission statement for apigateway.amazonaws.com. Choice A fails because the execution role controls what the function can call, not who can invoke the function.

quiz.q: A team wants to enable a new checkout flow for 10 percent of users at first, change the percentage later without redeploying the Lambda functions, reject malformed configuration before it goes live, and roll back automatically if an error alarm fires. Which approach meets these requirements?
choices: Store the percentage in a Lambda environment variable and publish a new function version each time the value changes, using CodeDeploy for rollback
Store a feature flag in AWS AppConfig with a validator, deploy it with a deployment strategy and alarm-based rollback, and read it through the AppConfig Agent extension
Store the percentage in an S3 object that every invocation downloads, and ask on-call engineers to restore the previous object version if the alarm fires
Create a separate API Gateway stage for the new flow and have the frontend send 10 percent of users to that stage URL by checking a cookie
quiz.explain: AppConfig is built for feature flags: validators block bad configuration, deployment strategies roll it out gradually, alarms trigger automatic rollback, and the Lambda extension caches the value. Choice A requires a code deployment for every change, which the team explicitly wants to avoid.

days.recap: Keep one artifact and vary only configuration: Parameter Store and Secrets Manager hierarchies, AppConfig for validated feature flags with rollback, API Gateway stages and stage variables, Lambda aliases (with per-alias permissions), unique container tags, Copilot environments and Amplify branch overrides.

days.title: Testing on AWS: SAM Local, CDK Assertions, Mock APIs, Test Events and AI-Generated Tests

concepts.heading: Local Testing with the AWS SAM CLI
concepts.body: The SAM CLI runs Lambda code locally in a container that emulates the Lambda runtime, so a developer can test logic without deploying. sam local invoke OrdersFunction -e events/order-created.json runs one function with a JSON event file and prints its logs and return value. sam local start-api serves the API routes from the template on a local port, so you can send real HTTP requests with curl, and sam local generate-event creates sample payloads, for example sam local generate-event s3 put or apigateway aws-proxy, which you then edit. sam validate checks the template, and sam validate --lint adds cfn-lint rules. Local runs still call real AWS services unless the code stubs them, so they use whatever credentials the profile provides. The exam signal is a fast feedback loop: test a small change locally with an event file instead of deploying to AWS every time.

concepts.heading: Validating Infrastructure Code with CDK, CloudFormation and SAM
concepts.body: Infrastructure code can be tested before any stack exists. In the AWS CDK, the assertions module turns a stack into a template with Template.fromStack(stack), and fine-grained tests check it, for example template.hasResourceProperties('AWS::Lambda::Function', {Runtime: 'nodejs20.x', Timeout: 10}) or template.resourceCountIs('AWS::SQS::Queue', 2); snapshot tests compare the whole synthesized template with a stored copy to catch unintended changes. For plain templates, aws cloudformation validate-template checks syntax, cfn-lint checks resource properties against the specification, and CloudFormation Guard rules check policy, such as every bucket having encryption. Before an update, a change set or cdk diff shows what will be added, modified or replaced. These tests run in CodeBuild on every commit. A question asking how to prove that synthesized infrastructure has a required property is pointing to CDK assertions.

concepts.heading: Mock APIs and Stubbed Dependencies
concepts.body: An API Gateway mock integration returns a response without calling any backend. You set the integration type to MOCK, the request mapping template selects a status code such as {"statusCode": 200}, and the integration response mapping template returns a fixed JSON body. A frontend or partner team can then build against the agreed contract while the real Lambda backend is still being written, and the integration is later switched to Lambda without changing the URL. Mocks are also useful for an external payment or shipping provider that has no sandbox or charges per call: the test environment points at a mock endpoint that returns success, decline or timeout responses on demand. Inside unit tests, the same idea applies to SDK calls, which are stubbed with a client mock library, botocore Stubber or moto. The exam signal: use mocks to remove external dependencies from tests, not to hide real integration problems.

concepts.heading: Building JSON Test Events for Lambda and API Gateway
concepts.body: A Lambda function receives a JSON event whose shape depends on the caller, so a useful test event matches that shape exactly. An API Gateway proxy event carries httpMethod, path, headers, queryStringParameters, pathParameters and a body that is a string, so JSON payloads must be stringified inside it; an SQS event has a Records array with body and messageId; an S3 event lists bucket.name and object.key. In the Lambda console you can save test events as private or shareable, so the whole team reuses the same cases. The API Gateway console Test feature sends a request through one method, including mapping templates, without a deployment. Good test sets include edge cases: an empty body, a missing path parameter, a malformed JSON string, a batch with one bad record. Questions about a handler that works in the console but fails behind API Gateway often come down to a test event that did not match the real event format.

concepts.heading: Unit Tests, Integration Tests and the Pipeline Gate
concepts.body: Unit tests check the function's own logic and should not call live AWS resources; when they hit a shared development table they become flaky, failing with ResourceNotFoundException in another account or with throttling when colleagues use the same table. Stub the SDK clients instead. Integration tests need real infrastructure, so the pipeline deploys a short-lived stack with SAM or CDK, runs the tests against it and tears it down. In AWS CodeBuild, a report group in the buildspec collects JUnit-style results and coverage files such as JaCoCo, Cobertura or LCOV, and any failing test returns a non-zero exit code that fails the build and stops CodePipeline before deployment. A typical order is unit tests in the build stage, deploy to staging, integration tests, optional manual approval, then production. Answers that retry flaky tests or skip the test stage are traps.

concepts.heading: AI-Generated Tests and Regression Automation with Kiro
concepts.body: AI tools such as Kiro can write tests quickly, but every test needs an oracle, the expected value. Tests generated only from the implementation encode what the code does today, bug included, so high coverage can hide defects. Generate tests from requirements or a Kiro spec's acceptance criteria, for example orders over 20 kg use the heavy rate, and have a reviewer check each assertion in the pull request. Give the tool the coverage report's uncovered branches plus the requirements, and record conventions such as unit tests never call AWS in a steering file; an agent hook can update tests whenever a handler file is saved. The pipeline still runs the full suite deterministically. AI can then help analyze results: an EventBridge rule on build completion invokes a Lambda function that sends only failed cases and their history to a Bedrock model and posts a triage summary to SNS, while the build status stays exactly as the tests set it.

examPoints: A question where a frontend team must build against an API before the backend exists is testing an API Gateway mock integration.

A question that asks how to assert that synthesized infrastructure contains a resource with specific properties is testing AWS CDK assertions (Template.fromStack with hasResourceProperties), not a manual console check.

A question where AI-generated tests pass but miss a known defect, or where an AI summary might change a build result, is testing that expected values come from requirements and that the deterministic test gate decides pass or fail.

quiz.q: A mobile team must start integrating with a new REST API next week, but the Lambda backend will not be ready for a month. The API contract, including response bodies, is already agreed. What lets the mobile team start immediately with the least effort?
choices: Create the API methods in API Gateway with a MOCK integration and integration response mapping templates that return the agreed JSON bodies
Deploy placeholder Lambda functions that sleep for one second and return random JSON so that the mobile team can measure realistic latency
Ask the mobile team to run sam local start-api on their laptops against the backend repository, which serves responses before any code exists
Create a CloudFront distribution with a static S3 origin that holds one JSON file per route and give the mobile team that distribution URL
quiz.explain: A mock integration returns the agreed responses with no backend, and the same API can later be switched to Lambda integrations without changing the URL. Choice C fails because sam local start-api runs the functions defined in the template, so it cannot serve responses for code that has not been written.

quiz.q: A developer asks Kiro to generate unit tests for a shipping-fee Lambda function. The 25 generated tests pass and line coverage reaches 92 percent, yet a week later customers report that parcels over 20 kg are charged the light rate, a bug that existed when the tests were generated. What should the developer change?
choices: Ask Kiro to keep adding tests until line coverage reaches 100 percent, because full coverage proves that every branch returns the correct fee
Replace the unit tests with end-to-end tests through API Gateway, because unit tests cannot detect calculation errors in Lambda functions
Generate the tests from the written requirements or a Kiro spec's acceptance criteria and have a reviewer check each assertion against them
Regenerate the suite several times with different prompts and keep the union of all runs so that variation eventually covers the faulty rule
quiz.explain: Tests generated from the existing code use its current output as the expected value, so they lock the bug in; requirement-based assertions reviewed by a person catch it. Choice A fails because coverage only shows that a line ran, not that its assertion is correct.

days.recap: Test fast with sam local and JSON events that match the real event shape, prove infrastructure with CDK assertions and template validation, remove external dependencies with mock integrations and SDK stubs, and treat AI-generated tests as code that needs requirement-based assertions, review and a deterministic pipeline gate.

days.title: Packaging and IaC Deployment: Lambda Packages, SAM and CloudFormation Templates, Change Sets and Stack Rollback

concepts.heading: .zip Packages and Lambda Layers
concepts.body: A .zip deployment package holds the handler code and its dependencies. It can be uploaded directly up to 50 MB zipped, or through S3, and the unzipped size of the function plus all its layers must stay within 250 MB. Layers package shared libraries or a common runtime dependency once and attach them to many functions, up to five layers per function, and each layer is versioned so a function pins a specific layer version. Layers reduce duplication and keep each function's own package small, which speeds up deployments, but they do not raise the 250 MB limit. Smaller packages also cold-start faster, so exclude tests and documentation and use bundlers such as esbuild for Node.js to drop unused code. On the exam, .zip with layers is the default for typical code, and the answer changes only when the dependencies genuinely exceed the size limits or the team needs container tooling.

concepts.heading: Container Images for Lambda
concepts.body: Lambda can run a function packaged as a container image of up to 10 GB stored in Amazon ECR. The image must include the Lambda Runtime Interface Client, which AWS base images for each runtime already contain, and the function points at one image built for one architecture, x86_64 or arm64; Lambda does not use multi-architecture manifest lists. Images suit large machine learning libraries or native toolchains that exceed the .zip limits, and teams that already build and scan Docker images in their pipeline. Layers cannot be attached to image-based functions, so shared code goes into the image's own layers instead, ordered so that dependencies come before the frequently changing application code to keep builds fast. Changing the image means updating the function to a new image URI or digest and publishing a new version. A scenario with a 2 GB dependency set points to a container image, not to a bigger .zip.

concepts.heading: AWS SAM Templates and the SAM Deployment Flow
concepts.body: A SAM template is a CloudFormation template with the line Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31, which lets short resource types such as AWS::Serverless::Function, AWS::Serverless::Api and AWS::Serverless::SimpleTable expand into full CloudFormation resources at deploy time. The Globals section sets shared properties such as Runtime, Timeout and environment variables for every function, and an Events block on a function creates its trigger and the needed permissions. sam build resolves dependencies and prepares the artifacts, and sam deploy uploads them to S3 or ECR, creates a CloudFormation change set and executes it; sam deploy --guided saves answers to samconfig.toml so later runs need no prompts. AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference add versioning and CodeDeploy traffic shifting with a few lines. Questions about defining a function, its API and its permissions in very little code are testing SAM.

concepts.heading: CloudFormation Templates for Repeatable Environments
concepts.body: A CloudFormation template declares the desired end state, and CloudFormation works out the API calls. Resources is the only required section; Parameters let one template serve dev and prod (for example an EnvName parameter with AllowedValues), Mappings hold lookup tables, Conditions decide whether a resource is created, and Outputs with an Export name share values such as a VPC ID with other stacks through Fn::ImportValue. Intrinsic functions such as !Sub, !Ref and !GetAtt build names and ARNs instead of hardcoding them. Secrets stay out of templates by using dynamic references like {{resolve:secretsmanager:prod/db:SecretString:password}}. DeletionPolicy: Retain or Snapshot protects stateful resources when a stack is deleted. Nested stacks package repeated pieces as child templates. The exam rewards one parameterized template deployed many times over copied templates per environment.

concepts.heading: Change Sets: Previewing an Update
concepts.body: A change set compares the current stack with a new template or parameter values and lists every planned action before anything changes: Add, Modify or Remove, and for modifications whether the resource will be replaced. The Replacement field is the key one, because replacing a DynamoDB table or an RDS instance creates a new resource and deletes the old one with its data; changing a property such as a table's key schema forces replacement. The workflow is aws cloudformation create-change-set, review with describe-change-set, then execute-change-set, and a pipeline can place a manual approval between creating and executing it. SAM uses change sets under the hood, and sam deploy --confirm-changeset pauses for review. CDK shows the same information with cdk diff. Any scenario that fears an update might destroy a stateful resource is asking for a change set review.

concepts.heading: Stack Rollback and Recovering a Failed Update
concepts.body: If any resource fails during stack creation or update, CloudFormation by default rolls back every change in that operation to the last known good state, and the stack events show the first CREATE_FAILED or UPDATE_FAILED event with the reason. Rollback triggers extend this: you list CloudWatch alarms and a monitoring period, and if an alarm fires during the update or the monitoring time afterwards, CloudFormation rolls the whole update back. For debugging a failed create, you can disable rollback so the successful resources stay in place while you fix the cause. If a rollback itself cannot complete, for example because a resource was changed outside CloudFormation, the stack sits in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED until you fix the resource and run continue-update-rollback, optionally skipping resources. Manual rollback means redeploying the previous template version from source control. Know that automatic rollback is the default, not something you must enable.

examPoints: A question with a Lambda dependency set larger than the 250 MB unzipped limit is testing container image packaging (up to 10 GB in ECR), while a question about sharing one library across many functions is testing layers.
A question that worries an update might replace a database or table is testing a change set review (Replacement column) before execution.

A question that wants an update reverted automatically when an error alarm fires shortly after deployment is testing CloudFormation rollback triggers; a stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED is testing continue-update-rollback.

quiz.q: A team deploys stack updates with CloudFormation. They want CloudFormation to undo an update automatically if the application's 5XX alarm goes into ALARM during the update or within 15 minutes after it completes. What should they configure?
choices: A DeletionPolicy of Snapshot on every stateful resource in the template so that CloudFormation restores them when the alarm fires
Rollback triggers on the stack that list the 5XX alarm with a monitoring time of 15 minutes
A stack policy that denies Update:Replace on all resources so that no update can change a resource that the alarm depends on
Termination protection on the stack together with an SNS notification topic that alerts the team when the alarm changes state
quiz.explain: Rollback triggers make CloudFormation monitor the listed alarms during the operation and for the monitoring period afterwards, and roll the update back if one fires. Choice C only blocks certain update actions; it does not revert an update that has already completed when an alarm fires.

quiz.q: A data science team must deploy a Lambda function whose Python dependencies, including native libraries, take 3 GB unzipped. They already build and scan Docker images in their pipeline. How should the function be packaged?
choices: Split the dependencies across five Lambda layers so that each layer stays below the 250 MB limit and attach all five to the function
Compress the .zip package with a higher compression level so that the upload stays under 50 MB and Lambda accepts the larger contents
Upload the dependencies to an S3 bucket and download them into /tmp in the handler on every invocation before running the code
Build a container image from an AWS Lambda base image, push it to Amazon ECR and create the function from that image
quiz.explain: Container images for Lambda can be up to 10 GB, fit the team's existing Docker build and scanning, and include the runtime interface client through the base image. Choice A fails because the 250 MB unzipped limit applies to the function and all of its layers combined.

days.recap: Package Lambda as .zip (with layers for shared code, 250 MB unzipped in total) or as a container image up to 10 GB, define serverless stacks with SAM and parameterized CloudFormation, review change sets for replacements, and rely on automatic rollback, rollback triggers and continue-update-rollback when updates fail.

days.title: Pipelines and Source Control: CodePipeline, CodeBuild, Branches, Tags and AI in CI/CD

concepts.heading: Invoking Pipelines from Linked Repositories
concepts.body: AWS CodePipeline models a release as stages, each with actions, and starts from a source action. For GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab or Bitbucket the source action uses a connection (AWS CodeConnections) that you authorize once; CodeCommit, S3 and ECR are also supported sources. Pipeline type V2 adds triggers with filters, so a pipeline can start only on pushes to main, only when files under services/orders/ change, or only when a Git tag matching v* is pushed, and pull request events can start a validation pipeline. The source artifact carries the commit ID, which later stages use for image tags or version descriptions. Execution modes decide what happens when commits arrive quickly: superseded lets a newer run replace an older one waiting at a stage, queued runs them in order. Questions about starting a release automatically from a repository event, without polling scripts, are testing CodePipeline triggers.

concepts.heading: Progressing Through Multiple Environments
concepts.body: A multi-environment pipeline builds once and promotes the same artifact: Source, Build, Deploy to dev, tests, Deploy to staging, integration tests, manual approval, Deploy to prod. Each deploy action uses the same template and image digest with different parameters, and for separate AWS accounts the pipeline assumes a cross-account deployment role in each target account, with the artifact bucket's KMS key shared to those accounts. A manual approval action pauses the pipeline, sends an SNS notification with a review link, and continues only when someone with permission calls PutApprovalResult with Approved; Rejected stops the run. Any failed action stops progression, so a failing test in staging never reaches production. Stage-level rollback can return a stage to the last successful execution. The exam favors promoting one tested artifact over rebuilding per environment, and an approval gate only where a human decision is required.

concepts.heading: CodeBuild and the buildspec
concepts.body: AWS CodeBuild runs each build in a fresh managed container defined by the project's image and compute type, driven by buildspec.yml. Phases run in order: install (runtimes and tools), pre_build (log in to ECR or CodeArtifact, run linters), build (compile, test, docker build) and post_build (push images, write imagedefinitions.json). The env section can pull values from Parameter Store with parameter-store and from Secrets Manager with secrets-manager, so no credential is written into the file, and exported-variables pass values such as an image tag to later pipeline actions. The artifacts section lists files for the next stage, reports defines test and coverage report groups, and cache (S3 or local, including Docker layer cache) speeds up repeated builds. aws codeartifact login points npm or pip at a private repository. A build fails when a command returns a non-zero exit code, which fails the pipeline action.

concepts.heading: Branches, Tags and Labels for Versions and Releases
concepts.body: Source control features describe which code is in which release. Feature branches isolate work until a pull request is reviewed and merged; a protected main branch requires reviews and passing checks; a release branch such as release/2.4 can receive only fixes while main moves on. A Git tag such as v2.4.0 is a fixed label on one commit, so it is the natural release identifier: a V2 pipeline trigger on tags matching v* builds and deploys exactly that commit, and the same value can become the container image tag and the Lambda version description. To roll back, redeploy the previous tag's artifact, which is faster and safer than reverting many commits under pressure. Semantic versioning (major.minor.patch) tells consumers whether a change is breaking. Exam scenarios that ask how to know which code is running, or how to release only approved snapshots, are testing tags and branch strategy.

concepts.heading: AI-Assisted Deployment Approvals
concepts.body: AI can shorten approval waits without becoming the control. A CloudFormation change set lists every planned action in structured form, including replacements, deletions and IAM changes, so fixed rules can decide risk: any IAM change, replacement or deletion waits for a human, while a change that only updates Lambda code or environment variables can be approved automatically by a Lambda function calling PutApprovalResult. An Amazon Bedrock model adds value by summarizing the change set in plain language for the approver and the audit trail, for example updates the code of three functions with no data resources affected. The model explains; it does not decide, and approving on the words low risk in a model answer is a trap. The function's permissions are limited to that one pipeline's approval action, and each automatic approval records the rule that allowed it.

concepts.heading: AI for Environment Provisioning and Post-Deployment Validation
concepts.body: Kiro can write AWS CDK or CloudFormation code for a preview environment per feature branch, but the output is still infrastructure as code: commit it, review the cdk diff in the pull request, and let the pipeline deploy it with a role limited to the preview account. Regenerating code from a prompt on every run is not repeatable, and an agent deploying from a laptop with an administrator profile breaks least privilege. After a release, deterministic signals guard production: CloudWatch alarms on the CodeDeploy deployment and PreTraffic or PostTraffic hooks roll a bad version back within minutes, even at night. AI then explains what happened: an alarm action can start a CloudWatch investigation that proposes root-cause hypotheses, and a Lambda function can send the failed build phase around the first error, the buildspec and the commit diff to a Bedrock model to suggest a fix with quoted evidence.

examPoints: A question that wants a pipeline to start only for a Git tag or a specific folder change is testing CodePipeline V2 triggers with filters on a repository connection.

A question about letting AI speed up approvals or validate deployments is testing the pattern where deterministic rules, alarms and hooks make the decision and the AI model only summarizes or explains.
A question about identifying exactly which code is in a release, or releasing a fixed snapshot, is testing Git tags as release labels and promotion of one built artifact.

quiz.q: A pipeline deploys CloudFormation change sets to production after a manual approval. Most change sets only update Lambda code, and approvers want routine changes approved automatically using a Lambda function that calls an Amazon Bedrock model. Which design keeps the approval step safe?
choices: The function sends each change set to the model and calls PutApprovalResult with Approved whenever the model's answer contains the words low risk
The function approves every change set immediately and asks the model to write a summary into the pipeline history for later review by approvers
Fixed rules on the change set send any IAM change, replacement or deletion to a human, approve only the rest, and attach the model's summary
The approval action is removed and CloudFormation asks the model before it creates, updates or deletes each resource in the production stack
quiz.explain: Risky change types are machine-readable in the change set, so deterministic rules decide what may be auto-approved and the model only explains the change. Choice A lets free-text model output decide, so a destructive change could be approved because of how one answer was worded.

quiz.q: A monorepo holds several services. The team wants the orders pipeline to run only when files under services/orders/ change on main, and the release pipeline to run only when a tag such as v3.2.0 is pushed. The repository is on GitHub. What should the developer configure?
choices: CodePipeline V2 pipelines with a GitHub connection source and triggers that filter on branch and file paths for one pipeline and on tags matching v* for the other
A scheduled EventBridge rule that starts both pipelines every five minutes and a first CodeBuild action in each that exits early when nothing relevant changed
One V1 pipeline per service that polls the repository and a manual approval action at the start of each pipeline where an engineer checks the changed paths
A GitHub webhook that calls a Lambda function to clone the repository, diff the commit and copy the changed folder to an S3 source bucket for each pipeline
quiz.explain: V2 pipeline triggers on a connection-based source filter by branch, file path and Git tag, so each pipeline starts only for the events it cares about. Choice B wastes builds, adds latency and moves trigger logic into custom code.

days.recap: CodePipeline starts from linked repositories with filtered triggers, promotes one artifact through environments with cross-account roles and approval gates, CodeBuild runs the buildspec phases, Git tags label releases, and AI tools summarize, provision and explain while rules, alarms and tests make the decisions.

days.title: Deployment Strategies and Rollback: CodeDeploy, ECS Task Definitions, EKS Manifests and Fargate

concepts.heading: Choosing a Deployment Strategy
concepts.body: Each strategy trades cost, speed and blast radius. All-at-once replaces everything together: fastest and cheapest, but every user sees a bad release and rollback means another full deployment. Rolling (in-place) replaces a batch at a time on existing capacity, so some capacity is temporarily out of service and old and new versions run together. Blue/green builds a separate green environment, shifts traffic when it is healthy and keeps blue for an instant rollback, at the cost of double capacity during the switch. Canary sends a small share, for example 10 percent, to the new version for a set time and then the rest; linear shifts equal steps at equal intervals, for example 10 percent every minute. Gradual strategies are only safe when something watches them, so pair them with alarms. Read the scenario's constraints, such as no downtime, instant rollback or limited spare capacity, and the strategy usually follows.

concepts.heading: CodeDeploy for Lambda: Alias Traffic Shifting
concepts.body: For Lambda, CodeDeploy shifts traffic between two versions behind an alias rather than replacing servers. With AWS SAM, AutoPublishAlias: live publishes a new version on each deploy, and DeploymentPreference sets the type, such as Canary10Percent10Minutes, Linear10PercentEvery1Minute or AllAtOnce. CodeDeploy first runs an optional PreTraffic hook, a Lambda function that tests the new version and reports Succeeded or Failed, then shifts the alias weights, then runs a PostTraffic hook. CloudWatch alarms listed in the deployment preference, for example on the new version's errors and p99 duration, make CodeDeploy stop and shift all traffic back to the old version if any alarm fires during the deployment. This works at 3 a.m. with nobody online. A scenario that wants a new Lambda version exposed to a small share of users and reverted automatically on errors is testing this setup.

concepts.heading: CodeDeploy for EC2 and Amazon ECS
concepts.body: On EC2 or on-premises servers the CodeDeploy agent runs an in-place deployment with configurations such as CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime, HalfAtATime or AllAtOnce, or a blue/green deployment that launches replacement instances behind the load balancer. The appspec.yml maps files to locations and runs scripts at lifecycle hooks such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart and ValidateService; a failing ValidateService script fails the deployment on that instance. For Amazon ECS, a CodeDeploy blue/green deployment registers the new task set in a second target group, can route a test listener to it first, and then shifts production traffic all at once, in a canary or linearly, with hooks such as AfterAllowTestTraffic for automated checks. Amazon ECS also offers built-in blue/green deployments managed by the ECS service itself. Deployment groups hold the targets, alarms and rollback settings.

concepts.heading: ECS Task Definitions, Fargate and Rolling Updates
concepts.body: A task definition revision describes the containers: image, CPU and memory, ports, environment, secrets, log configuration and roles. Fargate adds requirements: network mode must be awsvpc, so hostPort must equal containerPort or be omitted, and task-level CPU and memory must be a supported pair such as 256 CPU units and 512 MiB; options like privileged or placement constraints are rejected. A rolling update replaces tasks within two limits as percentages of the desired count: minimumHealthyPercent (floor, rounded up) and maximumPercent (ceiling, rounded down). With 6 tasks, 100 and 150 keep at least 6 healthy and start at most 3 extra at a time. The deployment circuit breaker with rollback returns the service to the last completed deployment if tasks keep failing. ECS resolves an image tag to a digest at each deployment, so moving a tag changes nothing until you start a new deployment.

concepts.heading: EKS Manifests and Kubernetes Rolling Updates
concepts.body: On Amazon EKS a Deployment manifest declares replicas, the pod template (image, resources, probes) and an update strategy, and kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml submits it. Changing the pod template, for example the image tag, creates a new ReplicaSet. Recreate deletes all old pods first and causes a gap. RollingUpdate, the default, works within maxSurge (extra pods above replicas, percentages round up) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed to be missing, percentages round down). With 10 replicas and room for only 2 extra pods, maxSurge 2 and maxUnavailable 0 keep 10 ready pods throughout, because a new pod counts only once its readiness probe passes. If new pods never become Ready, the rollout stalls and reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded after progressDeadlineSeconds, but Kubernetes does not roll back by itself; you run kubectl rollout undo deployment/api. Pods on Fargate profiles follow the same manifests.

concepts.heading: Automatic and Manual Rollback
concepts.body: Automatic rollback reacts without a person. CodeDeploy rolls back when a deployment fails or when an attached CloudWatch alarm fires, redeploying the last known good revision (for Lambda, by moving the alias back). CloudFormation rolls back a failed stack operation by default and, with rollback triggers, also on alarms during a monitoring period. The ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback enabled returns a service to its last completed deployment. AppConfig rolls back configuration on alarms. Manual rollback is a deliberate action: redeploy the previous revision or Git tag in CodeDeploy, point the Lambda alias at the previous version, update the ECS service to the previous task definition revision, or run kubectl rollout undo. Manual rollback suits problems that no alarm measures, such as a wrong business rule reported by users. Exam answers that rely on someone noticing are wrong when the requirement says automatic.

examPoints: A question that wants a new Lambda version to receive a small share of traffic and revert automatically on errors is testing a CodeDeploy canary or linear deployment preference with CloudWatch alarms.

A question that gives a desired task count, a minimum healthy count and a maximum number of extra tasks is testing ECS minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent (or Kubernetes maxSurge and maxUnavailable).
A question where a Fargate task definition fails validation is usually testing awsvpc network mode and task-level CPU and memory.

quiz.q: An ECS service on Fargate has a desired count of 6 and uses rolling updates. During deployments it must never have fewer than 6 healthy tasks, and to stay within the vCPU quota it must never run more than 3 extra tasks at a time. Which deployment configuration meets these requirements?
choices: minimumHealthyPercent 50 and maximumPercent 150
minimumHealthyPercent 100 and maximumPercent 100
minimumHealthyPercent 100 and maximumPercent 200
minimumHealthyPercent 100 and maximumPercent 150
quiz.explain: A floor of 100 percent keeps 6 healthy tasks and a ceiling of 150 percent allows at most 9 tasks, so ECS replaces 3 at a time. Choice B sets floor and ceiling both to 6, so ECS can neither start an extra task nor stop an old one and the deployment stalls.

quiz.q: A Kubernetes Deployment on Amazon EKS runs 10 replicas with readiness probes. A ResourceQuota leaves room for only 2 additional pods, and the service must keep at least 10 ready pods during every rollout. Which update strategy should the manifest use?
choices: RollingUpdate with maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 2
RollingUpdate with maxSurge 2 and maxUnavailable 0
RollingUpdate with the default maxSurge and maxUnavailable
Recreate with progressDeadlineSeconds set to 120
quiz.explain: maxSurge 2 fits the quota and maxUnavailable 0 removes an old pod only after a new one passes readiness, so ready capacity never falls below 10. Choice C uses the 25 percent defaults, which allow 3 extra pods and 2 unavailable pods, breaking both limits.

days.recap: Pick the strategy from the constraints (downtime, rollback speed, spare capacity), use CodeDeploy alias shifting with hooks and alarms for Lambda, blue/green or rolling updates for ECS and EKS with the right floor and ceiling, meet Fargate task definition rules, and know which services roll back automatically and how to roll back by hand.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Testing and Deployment

concepts.heading: Artifacts and Container Images Recap
concepts.body: Build once and promote the same artifact. Dependencies are pinned and bundled at build time, while environment-specific values arrive at run time. Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source and use multi-stage builds so the final image holds only the runtime and the built output. ECR images are tagged by commit SHA, protected with IMMUTABLE or IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION for moving environment tags, promoted by retagging the manifest (batch-get-image and put-image) so the digest never changes, and pushed from CodeBuild after aws ecr get-login-password. Lifecycle policies expire only what they select, and enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector continuously checks OS and language packages. When a scenario shows a large image, a slow rebuild, a failed push or an overwritten tag, return to these rules and the answer is usually visible in the first sentence of the stem.

concepts.heading: Environments and Configuration Recap
concepts.body: Environments differ in configuration, not in code. Parameter Store hierarchies and Secrets Manager hold per environment values; AWS AppConfig deploys feature flags and configuration with validators, gradual strategies and alarm-based rollback. API Gateway stages give each environment its own URL and stage variables, custom domains with base path mappings hide stage names, and endpoint types decide where the API is reachable. Lambda aliases point at immutable versions, can split traffic, and each alias needs its own invoke permission when a stage variable selects it. Containers select environments by image tag or digest and task definition revision, AWS Copilot creates named environments from one manifest, and Amplify builds each Git branch with app-level variables plus branch overrides. The recurring exam trap is any answer that rebuilds the artifact, duplicates a whole app, or hardcodes values per environment.

concepts.heading: Testing Recap
concepts.body: Fast feedback comes from sam local invoke with JSON events that match the real event shape, sam local start-api for HTTP routes, and the console test features. Infrastructure is tested before deployment with CDK assertions (Template.fromStack, hasResourceProperties, snapshot tests), validate-template, cfn-lint and Guard rules. Mock integrations in API Gateway let consumers build against a contract before the backend exists, and SDK stubs keep unit tests independent of live tables. Integration tests run against a short-lived stack, and CodeBuild report groups plus a non-zero exit code make the test stage a real gate. AI-generated tests need expected values from requirements or specs, human review of assertions, steering files for team conventions, and a pipeline that decides pass or fail deterministically while an AI summary only helps people triage failures.

concepts.heading: Packaging and Infrastructure as Code Recap
concepts.body: Lambda code ships as a .zip (50 MB zipped direct upload, 250 MB unzipped including up to five layers) or as a container image up to 10 GB in ECR, built for one architecture. SAM templates use the Serverless transform, Globals and Events to define functions, APIs and permissions in a few lines, and sam deploy creates and executes a change set. CloudFormation templates are parameterized for reuse, use dynamic references for secrets, and protect data with DeletionPolicy. Change sets reveal replacements before execution. Failed operations roll back automatically, rollback triggers add alarm-based rollback during a monitoring period, and continue-update-rollback recovers a stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. When an exam option suggests editing resources in the console to fix a stack, it is usually creating drift and the next deployment's rollback problem rather than solving anything.

concepts.heading: Pipelines, Source Control and AI in CI/CD Recap
concepts.body: CodePipeline starts from a repository connection or other source, and V2 triggers filter on branches, file paths and Git tags. Stages promote one artifact through dev, staging and prod with cross-account roles, automated tests and a manual approval where a human decision is needed. CodeBuild runs install, pre_build, build and post_build phases, reads secrets from Parameter Store or Secrets Manager, exports variables and publishes test reports. Git tags label releases and drive rollbacks. AI fits around these controls: Kiro writes IaC that is still reviewed with cdk diff and deployed by a scoped pipeline role, a Bedrock summary helps an approver while fixed rules on the change set decide auto-approval, and CloudWatch investigations or a Bedrock prompt with the failing build phase, buildspec and diff explain failures. Decisions stay deterministic.

concepts.heading: Deployment Strategies and Rollback Recap
concepts.body: All-at-once is fast with full blast radius, rolling saves capacity but mixes versions, blue/green doubles capacity for an instant switch back, canary tests a slice first and linear shifts in equal steps. CodeDeploy shifts Lambda alias weights with PreTraffic and PostTraffic hooks and alarm rollback, runs appspec hooks on EC2, and performs ECS blue/green with two target groups. ECS rolling updates are controlled by minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent, with a circuit breaker for automatic rollback, and Fargate requires awsvpc and task-level CPU and memory. EKS Deployments use maxSurge and maxUnavailable gated by readiness probes, and rollback there is kubectl rollout undo. Automatic rollback needs an alarm or failure signal; manual rollback redeploys the previous revision, tag or task definition. Match each requirement word in the stem to one of these mechanisms.

examPoints: When a Domain 3 question mentions environments, first ask whether the answer keeps one artifact and changes only configuration; options that rebuild or duplicate per environment are usually distractors.
When a question involves AI in testing or deployment, the correct option keeps tests, rules and alarms as the deciding gate and uses the AI tool to generate, summarize or explain.

quiz.q: A team runs a production pipeline that builds a container image, tests it in staging and deploys it to production. Auditors require proof that production runs exactly the bytes that passed staging tests. Which practice provides this?
choices: Rebuild the image in the production stage from the same commit and tag it prod so that the build inputs match the tested image
Promote the tested image by adding a production tag to its existing manifest in ECR and deploy it by digest
Keep a single mutable latest tag in ECR and redeploy the production service whenever the staging service is updated
Store the Dockerfile in the release notes and ask an approver to compare it with the one used in staging before each deploy
quiz.explain: Retagging the existing manifest keeps the same digest, which identifies exact image content, so production provably runs the tested image. Choice A can produce a different digest if a base image or unpinned dependency changed between builds.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly matches a requirement to the deployment mechanism that satisfies it?
choices: Shift 10 percent of Lambda traffic for 10 minutes and then the rest, rolling back on alarms: an ECS rolling update with maximumPercent 110
Preview whether an update will replace a DynamoDB table before anything changes: a CloudFormation rollback trigger on the stack
Keep 10 ready pods while replacing an EKS Deployment with only 2 spare pod slots: RollingUpdate with maxSurge 2 and maxUnavailable 0
Return a Kubernetes Deployment to its previous ReplicaSet automatically when new pods never become Ready: progressDeadlineSeconds alone
quiz.explain: maxSurge 2 fits the spare capacity and maxUnavailable 0 keeps all 10 ready pods, which matches the requirement exactly. Choice B confuses rollback triggers, which react to alarms during an update, with change sets, which preview replacements before execution.

days.recap: Domain 3 in one line: build once and promote one artifact, vary only configuration per environment, test locally and in the pipeline with deterministic gates, deploy through IaC with change sets, and pick the deployment strategy and rollback mechanism that the scenario's constraints demand.

days.title: Root Cause Analysis: Metrics, Logs, Traces, Logs Insights and AI-Assisted Error Analysis

concepts.heading: Reading Metrics, Logs and Traces Together
concepts.body: Each signal answers a different question. Metrics say what changed and when: for Lambda, Errors, Throttles, Duration, ConcurrentExecutions and IteratorAge for stream sources; for SQS, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage; for API Gateway, 4XXError, 5XXError, Latency and IntegrationLatency. Logs say why: the exception, the input and the request ID. Traces say where: an X-Ray trace shows how long each hop took and which downstream call failed. Every Lambda invocation also writes a REPORT line with Duration, Billed Duration, Memory Size, Max Memory Used and, on cold starts, Init Duration. A good investigation starts with the metric that moved, narrows the time window, then reads the logs and traces for requests in that window, joined by a request or correlation ID. Exam stems often hide the key clue in one metric, such as rising IteratorAge or Latency much higher than IntegrationLatency.

concepts.heading: Querying Logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights
concepts.body: Logs Insights queries one or more log groups with a pipeline of commands. fields picks fields, filter selects events, parse extracts values from unstructured text, stats aggregates and sort and limit shape the output. For example, filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count(*) by bin(5m) shows when errors started, and filter @type = "REPORT" | stats max(@maxMemoryUsed), avg(@duration) summarizes Lambda performance. JSON log fields are discovered automatically, so structured logs can be filtered as fields like level or orderId. The pattern command groups similar messages and returns each pattern with a count, which turns millions of lines into a short list. Generate query writes a query from a plain-English prompt, which needs the cloudwatch:GenerateQuery permission, and the result is a draft to check before trusting it. Use Insights for ad hoc questions; use metric filters for ongoing alarms.

concepts.heading: Debugging Service Integration Errors
concepts.body: Many defects sit between services rather than inside code. AccessDenied or AccessDeniedException means a missing identity or resource policy statement, a KMS key policy, or an explicit deny; CloudTrail shows which principal made the call and the error code. In API Gateway, a 502 with a Lambda proxy integration usually means the function returned a malformed response (it must return statusCode and a string body), while a 504 means the integration exceeded its timeout, 29 seconds by default for REST APIs. Throttling shows up as HTTP 429 from API Gateway, ThrottlingException or ProvisionedThroughputExceededException from AWS APIs, and the Throttles metric in Lambda; the fix is retries with exponential backoff and jitter, more capacity or less concurrency. A Lambda Task timed out message means the timeout was reached, often because a function in a VPC has no route to a public endpoint.

concepts.heading: Troubleshooting Deployment Failures from Output Logs
concepts.body: Every deployment tool records why it failed. In CloudFormation, read stack events from the oldest failure: the first CREATE_FAILED or UPDATE_FAILED event holds the real reason, while later events only describe the rollback. CodeBuild logs show the failing phase (install, pre_build, build or post_build) and the command that returned a non-zero exit code; read around the first error, not the last line. CodeDeploy shows which lifecycle event failed, and on EC2 the agent log at /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/deployment-logs/codedeploy-agent-deployments.log has the script output. For ECS, a stopped task's stoppedReason reports issues such as CannotPullContainerError (missing ECR permission or route) or an essential container that exited, and the service events list deployment problems. On EKS, kubectl describe pod shows ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff or failing probes. Questions give these strings as clues.

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Investigations
concepts.body: CloudWatch investigations is a generative AI feature that, during an incident, scans metrics, logs, traces, deployment events, AWS Health events and CloudTrail change events and proposes observations and root-cause hypotheses that engineers accept or discard. Without configuration, an investigation is started by a user, uses that user's permissions, is visible only to them and is deleted after 24 hours. Creating an investigation group (one per account) sets the IAM role the investigations use, retention from 7 to 90 days and encryption, makes investigations available to everyone with the right permissions, and lets a CloudWatch alarm action start an investigation automatically. Better telemetry gives better hypotheses: X-Ray traces or Application Signals for topology, and CloudTrail management events sent to CloudWatch Logs in the same Region, or access to CloudTrail Event history, for recent changes. The investigation role needs read access, not permission to change resources.

concepts.heading: AI-Assisted Error Analysis with Kiro and Amazon Bedrock
concepts.body: An AI tool can reason only over the context it receives. Pasting just NullPointerException into Kiro gets generic advice; giving it the full stack trace with the repository open, the log lines and X-Ray trace of one failing request, and the recent diff lets it tie a hypothesis to specific lines. Ask for a unit test that reproduces the defect: if the test fails before the fix and passes after, the hypothesis is confirmed and the test stays as a regression check. None of this needs production write access. For error volume, reduce before you ask: a Logs Insights query with filter and pattern turns 2 million error lines into a few dozen patterns with counts, and a scheduled Lambda function sends the top patterns and a few sample stack traces to a Bedrock model for a ranked report with next steps. Sending raw logs exceeds the context window and costs more.

examPoints: A question that asks when an error started and how often it occurs across large log groups is testing CloudWatch Logs Insights (filter and stats, or pattern for grouping), not downloading log files.
A question where a stack update fails and the console shows many rollback events is testing reading the first CREATE_FAILED or UPDATE_FAILED event for the real cause.
A question that wants AI-generated root-cause hypotheses to start automatically on an alarm and be shared with the team is testing a CloudWatch investigations group and an alarm investigation action.

quiz.q: An API Gateway REST API with a Lambda proxy integration returns HTTP 502 to every client. The Lambda function's logs show it completes successfully in 40 ms and returns the JSON object {"orderId": "123", "status": "ok"}. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The function returns a plain object instead of a proxy response with statusCode and a string body, so API Gateway cannot map it
The function exceeds the 29-second integration timeout, so API Gateway gives up on the call and returns a gateway error
The account's Lambda concurrency limit is reached, so API Gateway receives throttling errors and converts them to HTTP 502
The function's execution role lacks permission to write to CloudWatch Logs, so API Gateway rejects the response as unauthorized
quiz.explain: With a proxy integration the function must return an object with statusCode, optional headers and a string body; anything else is a malformed response and API Gateway returns 502. Choice B fails because the logs show a 40 ms run, and a timeout would produce a 504 rather than a 502.

quiz.q: A team wants a daily AI-written summary of the main error types across 40 Lambda functions that log about 2 million error lines a day. A prototype that sent all raw lines to an Amazon Bedrock model exceeded the context window and was expensive. Which redesign is most effective?
choices: Split the lines into chunks that fit the context window, send every chunk to the model in parallel, and concatenate all of the answers
Fine-tune a Bedrock model each week on the previous month of error logs and ask it each morning which errors happened yesterday
Send only the first 1,000 error lines after midnight to the model, because the earliest errors represent every error type of the day
Group the error lines with a Logs Insights query that uses the pattern command, then send the top patterns, counts and sample traces to the model
quiz.explain: The pattern command compresses millions of lines into representative patterns with exact counts, so the model receives every error type in a small, cheap prompt. Choice A still pays to send all 2 million lines and produces duplicated, inconsistent descriptions of the same errors.

days.recap: Find the metric that moved, query the logs with Logs Insights, follow traces to the failing hop, read the first failure in deployment logs, and use AI tools such as CloudWatch investigations, Kiro and Bedrock with rich, reduced context and a reproducing test to confirm the cause.

days.title: Logging, Custom Metrics, Alerts, Tracing and Health Checks

concepts.heading: Structured Logging for Application Events
concepts.body: Structured logs write each event as JSON with consistent fields instead of free text, for example {"level":"ERROR","requestId":"c1f2...","orderId":"o-981","action":"checkout","durationMs":412}. Logs Insights discovers these fields automatically, so you can filter by orderId or count by action without parse expressions. Include a correlation ID that travels through every service a request touches, record user actions and state changes at INFO, and keep DEBUG off in production. Lambda's advanced logging controls can emit the function's logs in JSON and filter them by application and system log level without code changes, and libraries such as Powertools for AWS Lambda add request context automatically. Never log secrets or raw personal data; a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy can detect and mask PII in log events. Set a retention period on each log group, because the default is to keep logs forever.

concepts.heading: Emitting Custom Metrics
concepts.body: Business and application metrics, such as orders placed or payment failures, are not published by AWS, so code must emit them. The PutMetricData API sends values with a namespace, metric name, dimensions and unit; it is a synchronous API call per batch, so high-volume code should batch values. The Embedded Metric Format is often better: the code writes a JSON log line containing an _aws object that declares the namespace, dimensions and metrics, and CloudWatch extracts the metrics asynchronously from the log without an extra API call, while the full event stays searchable in the logs. Dimensions create a separate metric for each unique combination, so never use high-cardinality values such as user IDs or request IDs as dimensions; put those in the log fields instead. High-resolution metrics with a StorageResolution of 1 second support alarms on faster periods when needed.

concepts.heading: Notification Alerts for Quotas and Deployments
concepts.body: A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric or metric math expression and, on ALARM, notifies an SNS topic or triggers an action. Quota alerts use usage metrics in the AWS/Usage namespace with the SERVICE_QUOTA function: e1 = m1/SERVICE_QUOTA(m1)*100 and an alarm on e1 above 70 for 5 minutes warns before throttling, and it follows quota increases automatically. Alerts for specific actions come from EventBridge: CodeDeploy emits CodeDeploy Deployment State-change Notification events with states such as SUCCESS and FAILURE, and CodePipeline emits Pipeline Execution State Change events, all on the default event bus of the Region where the resource runs, with no CloudTrail trail needed. An event pattern on source aws.codedeploy and those states targets an SNS topic, whose access policy must let events.amazonaws.com publish when the topic was created outside the console. API-call events from CloudTrail cannot report an outcome.

concepts.heading: Distributed Tracing with X-Ray and OpenTelemetry
concepts.body: A trace follows one request across services using a trace ID passed in the X-Amzn-Trace-Id header or OpenTelemetry context. Each service records a segment, and calls inside it become subsegments with timings, so a slow DynamoDB or HTTP call stands out. Lambda enables tracing with active tracing in the function configuration, and API Gateway can start traces at the stage. Annotations are indexed key-value pairs used to search traces, for example customerId = 42; metadata holds unindexed detail. Sampling rules limit cost by tracing a reservoir per second plus a percentage. The trace map shows services and their error and latency. AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) is the AWS supported OpenTelemetry distribution: instrument once with OpenTelemetry APIs, use the ADOT Lambda layer or collector, and send traces to X-Ray and metrics to CloudWatch. The X-Ray SDKs and daemon entered maintenance mode (security fixes only) on February 25, 2026, and AWS recommends migrating to OpenTelemetry.

concepts.heading: Application Health Checks
concepts.body: Health checks decide whether an instance or task should receive traffic or be replaced. An Application Load Balancer target group sends HTTP requests to a path such as /health from outside and stops routing to targets that fail the healthy threshold. An ECS container health check is different: it is a command that runs inside the container, for example CMD-SHELL with curl, and if an essential container becomes UNHEALTHY the service scheduler replaces the task. Every binary the command uses must exist in the image, so minimal or distroless images need the CMD form with a bundled health binary. ECS uses only the check in the task definition, not a Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK. A health endpoint should check the process itself and return quickly. For service-level health, CloudWatch Application Signals tracks latency, faults and errors against service level objectives, and Route 53 health checks can drive DNS failover.

concepts.heading: Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes
concepts.body: Kubernetes on Amazon EKS runs three kinds of probes per container. A liveness probe asks whether the process is stuck; repeated failures restart the container. A readiness probe asks whether the pod should get traffic now; failures remove it from Service endpoints, and from load balancer targets that use IP mode, without a restart. A startup probe asks whether the app has finished starting; until it succeeds, liveness and readiness are disabled, and it allows up to failureThreshold times periodSeconds, for example 18 times 10 seconds for 3 minutes. Two classic mistakes appear in exam stems: a liveness probe that fires before a slow app is up, causing endless restarts (CrashLoopBackOff), fixed with a startup probe; and probes that check an external database, so a failover makes every pod fail at once and the whole fleet restarts. Keep liveness about the process itself.

examPoints: A question that wants business metrics from high-volume Lambda code without extra API calls is testing the Embedded Metric Format; a question about cost spikes from per-user dimensions is testing metric cardinality.
A question that wants a notification when a deployment finishes or when usage nears a quota is testing EventBridge service state-change events to SNS, or an alarm using SERVICE_QUOTA metric math.
A question where pods restart during slow startup or all restart during a database failover is testing startup probes and keeping liveness probes free of external dependencies.

quiz.q: A developer must email the team through an SNS topic whenever a CodeDeploy deployment in us-east-1 finishes, stating whether it succeeded or failed. The topic was created with the AWS CLI and has its default access policy. The developer creates an EventBridge rule with the topic as target and no execution role. Which TWO steps are required? Choose the option that lists both.
choices: Create a CloudTrail trail in us-east-1, and match detail-type AWS API Call via CloudTrail with eventName CreateDeployment
Create the rule on the default event bus in us-west-2, and add an IAM execution role to the rule's SNS target with sns:Publish
Match source aws.codedeploy with detail-type CodeDeploy Deployment State-change Notification and states SUCCESS or FAILURE, and allow events.amazonaws.com to publish in the topic policy
Match source aws.codedeploy with any detail-type, and add a subscription filter policy on the email subscription that drops START events
quiz.explain: CodeDeploy emits deployment state-change events natively, so a pattern on SUCCESS and FAILURE fires exactly when deployments finish, and a CLI-created topic needs a policy statement for events.amazonaws.com. Choice A fails because the CreateDeployment API call event fires when the deployment is requested, before any result exists.

quiz.q: A Java API on Amazon EKS needs about 2 minutes to load a cache at startup. Its liveness probe calls /health, which also queries the database, with initialDelaySeconds 10. New pods restart repeatedly during rollouts, and every pod restarted at once during a database failover. Which change set fixes both problems?
choices: Move the database check into a readiness probe and set restartPolicy to Never in the Deployment's pod template
Add a startup probe that covers the 2-minute startup and make the liveness probe check only that the process itself responds
Raise the liveness probe timeoutSeconds to 120 seconds and keep the database check so that slow responses no longer count as failures
Remove all probes from the Deployment and rely on the Application Load Balancer target group health check to replace failing pods
quiz.explain: A startup probe disables liveness until the app has started, and a liveness probe that checks only the process no longer fails on every pod when the database fails over. Choice A is invalid because Deployments only accept restartPolicy Always, and a readiness check on the database would still pull every pod out of service at once.

days.recap: Log structured JSON with correlation IDs, emit custom metrics with EMF or PutMetricData while watching cardinality, alert on quotas with SERVICE_QUOTA and on deployments with EventBridge state-change events, trace with X-Ray or ADOT, and design health checks and probes that check the right thing at the right time.

days.title: Performance Optimization: Concurrency, Connection Pooling, Memory, Messaging, Caching and Bottlenecks

concepts.heading: Concurrency: Provisioned, Reserved and Scaling Out
concepts.body: Lambda concurrency is the number of requests being handled at the same moment. Reserved concurrency sets both a guaranteed share and a maximum for one function, which protects a downstream database from too many parallel connections. Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of execution environments initialized ahead of time, which removes cold start latency for predictable traffic; it costs money while configured, can be scheduled with Application Auto Scaling, and applies to a version or alias, not $LATEST. Lambda SnapStart reduces startup time for supported runtimes by restoring a snapshot of an initialized environment. On EC2, an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy, for example average CPU at 50 percent, adds and removes instances as load changes. Exam signals: latency spikes on the first requests after idle point to provisioned concurrency; a downstream overload points to reserved concurrency.

concepts.heading: Connection Pooling and Thread Pools
concepts.body: Opening a database connection is slow, and databases support a limited number of them. In Lambda, create SDK clients and database connections outside the handler so that warm invocations reuse them; a client created inside the handler pays the setup cost every time. Thousands of concurrent Lambda environments can still exhaust a relational database's connections, which is what Amazon RDS Proxy solves: it pools and shares connections in front of RDS or Aurora, absorbs bursts, and can use IAM authentication and Secrets Manager credentials. In long-running services on EC2 or containers, an application-side connection pool and a bounded thread pool keep work in parallel without overwhelming dependencies, and HTTP keep-alive reuses TCP and TLS connections to AWS endpoints. A scenario with too many connections errors during a traffic spike from Lambda is testing RDS Proxy, not a bigger database instance.

concepts.heading: Optimizing Memory and Compute
concepts.body: Lambda memory ranges from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, and CPU is allocated in proportion, so raising memory often shortens CPU-bound functions enough that the cost per invocation stays flat or falls. The REPORT line shows Max Memory Used against Memory Size, and a Logs Insights query over @maxMemoryUsed and @memorySize finds over-provisioned functions. AWS Compute Optimizer recommends Lambda memory from the last 14 days of usage, with estimated savings and a performance risk rating, for functions configured at 1,792 MB or less with at least 50 invocations; others show as Unavailable. The open-source Lambda Power Tuning tool runs a function at several memory sizes and plots cost against speed. The arm64 architecture on Graviton often gives better price performance. For EC2 and containers, rightsize from CloudWatch and Container Insights data. Apply changes through IaC and confirm duration afterwards.

concepts.heading: Optimizing Messaging with SQS and SNS
concepts.body: Messaging performance depends on fewer, fuller calls. SQS long polling, with ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds or WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds, waits for messages instead of returning empty responses, cutting empty receives and cost. Batch APIs send, receive or delete up to 10 messages per call. For a Lambda event source mapping, a larger batch size and a batching window let one invocation process many messages, partial batch responses retry only the failed ones, and the queue's visibility timeout should be at least six times the function timeout so messages do not reappear while being processed. For fan-out, an SNS topic delivers each message to several SQS queues, and subscription filter policies send each consumer only the messages it needs, which avoids filtering in code. When a backlog grows, watch ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage and raise consumer concurrency or batch size.

concepts.heading: Caching with ElastiCache, DAX and CloudFront
concepts.body: Caching moves repeated reads closer to the caller. With Amazon ElastiCache, lazy loading (cache-aside) reads the cache first and on a miss reads the database and stores the result with a TTL, so only requested data is cached but the first read is slow; write-through updates the cache on every write, so data is fresh but some cached items are never read. A TTL limits staleness in both patterns. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that serves eventually consistent reads in microseconds with almost no code change, since the DAX client uses the same API; strongly consistent reads pass through to the table. Amazon CloudFront caches responses at edge locations according to cache policies, and a low cache hit ratio usually means the cache key includes headers, cookies or query strings that vary needlessly. API Gateway stage caching suits repeated identical API requests.

concepts.heading: Detecting Bottlenecks and Using AI Tools to Optimize
concepts.body: Find the bottleneck before changing anything. CloudWatch metrics show saturation (Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions, CPU, queue age), Lambda Insights and Container Insights add memory and CPU detail, X-Ray subsegments split handler time, and CloudWatch Application Signals breaks service latency down by dependency, for example a DynamoDB Scan on one table. AI tools then help fix it: give Kiro the code, the table key schema and the measured breakdown, and ask for targeted changes such as replacing a Scan with a Query on an index or moving client creation out of the handler. Review AI refactors against the API's contract; replacing GetItem loops with BatchGetItem is faster but must retry UnprocessedKeys with backoff, or items silently disappear under load. Accept a change only when unit tests still pass and a repeatable load test shows better p95 latency.

examPoints: A question about too many database connections from Lambda during spikes is testing RDS Proxy and reusing connections outside the handler; a question about cold-start latency for predictable traffic is testing provisioned concurrency.
A question that asks for usage-based memory recommendations across many Lambda functions is testing AWS Compute Optimizer, including its 1,792 MB and 50-invocation limits.
A question about many empty SQS receives, high SQS cost or a slow cache hit ratio is testing long polling and batching, or cache key and TTL design.

quiz.q: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. During flash sales, Lambda scales to 2,000 concurrent executions and the database rejects connections with too many clients errors, although its CPU stays low. What should the developer do first?
choices: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the database, connect through the proxy, and create the connection outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it
Move the database to a larger instance class with more memory so that the max_connections setting rises enough for 2,000 concurrent executions
Enable provisioned concurrency of 2,000 on the function so that every execution environment opens its database connection before the sale
Open and close a new database connection inside the handler on every invocation so that idle connections are released as quickly as possible
quiz.explain: RDS Proxy pools and shares connections in front of the database, and reusing connections outside the handler avoids a new connection per invocation. Choice C keeps 2,000 environments warm, each still holding its own connection, so the database runs out of connections just the same while costs rise.

quiz.q: A Lambda function configured with 3,008 MB runs thousands of times a day, but AWS Compute Optimizer shows no memory recommendation for it. The developer suspects it is over-provisioned. What explains this, and how can the developer check real memory use?
choices: Compute Optimizer needs the CloudWatch agent inside the function; add the agent as a layer and wait 14 days for the first recommendation
Compute Optimizer only analyzes functions with provisioned concurrency; enable it for 14 days and then read the memory recommendation
Compute Optimizer only covers container image functions; repackage the .zip package as an image and wait for the next daily refresh
Compute Optimizer skips functions above 1,792 MB; query the REPORT lines in Logs Insights to compare @maxMemoryUsed with @memorySize
quiz.explain: Lambda memory recommendations cover only functions configured at 1,792 MB or less, and the REPORT line fields show peak memory used against the configured size. Choice A fails because Compute Optimizer needs no agent for Lambda; the function is excluded because of its memory setting.

days.recap: Use reserved and provisioned concurrency for control and latency, RDS Proxy and reused clients for connections, Compute Optimizer and REPORT data to size memory, long polling, batching and SNS filters for messaging, the right cache for each layer, and measured evidence before and after any AI-suggested optimization.

days.title: Domain 4 Review: Troubleshooting and Optimization

concepts.heading: Root Cause Analysis Recap
concepts.body: Start from the metric that changed, narrow the time window, then read logs and traces for requests in that window. Lambda's REPORT line, API Gateway's Latency versus IntegrationLatency, IteratorAge and queue age each point to a different layer. Logs Insights answers when and how often with filter, stats and pattern, and Generate query drafts queries from plain English with the cloudwatch:GenerateQuery permission. Integration errors have signatures: AccessDenied for policies, 502 for malformed proxy responses, 504 for integration timeouts, 429 and ThrottlingException for rate limits. Deployment failures are explained by the first failed CloudFormation event, the failing CodeBuild phase, the CodeDeploy lifecycle event and agent log, ECS stoppedReason and kubectl describe pod. When a stem quotes an error string, that string is the clue: map it to its layer before reading the options.

concepts.heading: Logging and Metrics Recap
concepts.body: Structured JSON logs with a correlation ID make every field queryable, Lambda's advanced logging controls set JSON format and log levels without code changes, data protection policies mask PII, and every log group needs a retention period. Custom metrics come from PutMetricData, which is an API call per batch, or the Embedded Metric Format, which extracts metrics from log lines asynchronously. Dimensions multiply metrics, so identifiers that are unique per user or request belong in log fields, not dimensions. Alarms send notifications to SNS and can start actions; metric math with SERVICE_QUOTA warns before a quota is reached. For alerts on specific actions such as a finished deployment, use native service state-change events on EventBridge, and remember the SNS topic policy that lets EventBridge publish. These pieces answer most monitoring design questions on the exam.

concepts.heading: Tracing and Health Recap
concepts.body: X-Ray traces follow a request through services with segments and subsegments, annotations make traces searchable, metadata stores unindexed detail, sampling rules control cost, and the trace map shows where errors and latency gather. AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry instruments code once with OpenTelemetry and sends traces to X-Ray and metrics to CloudWatch. Application Signals adds service-level metrics, dependencies and SLOs. Health checks come in layers: ALB target groups probe from outside, ECS container health checks run commands inside the image, and Kubernetes uses liveness to restart stuck processes, readiness to gate traffic and startup probes for slow starts. The repeated mistake to recognize is a health check that depends on an external system or on a binary missing from the image, which turns one problem into a fleet-wide restart.

concepts.heading: Optimization Recap
concepts.body: Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees, provisioned concurrency removes cold starts for predictable traffic, and SnapStart shortens startup for supported runtimes; EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking follows load. Reuse clients and connections outside the handler and put RDS Proxy in front of relational databases that Lambda hits in bursts. Size Lambda memory from evidence, since CPU scales with it, using REPORT data, Compute Optimizer for functions up to 1,792 MB, or Power Tuning, and consider arm64. Make messaging efficient with long polling, batches of up to 10, event source mapping batch size and windows, a visibility timeout well above the function timeout, and SNS filter policies for fan-out. Choose caches by layer: ElastiCache with lazy loading or write-through, DAX for DynamoDB reads, CloudFront and API Gateway caching at the edge and API.

concepts.heading: AI Tools in Troubleshooting and Optimization Recap
concepts.body: DVA-C03 expects you to use AI tools well, not blindly. CloudWatch investigations generates hypotheses from metrics, logs, traces and change events; an investigation group, alarm actions and CloudTrail events in CloudWatch Logs in the same Region make it automatic, shared and change-aware, and its role stays read-only. Kiro analyzes failures best with the full stack trace, the code, request-level logs and traces and the recent diff, and its hypotheses are confirmed with a reproducing test. Bedrock prompts for error reports should carry reduced data such as Logs Insights patterns with counts. For optimization, give the tool measured evidence, review its changes against API contracts such as BatchGetItem UnprocessedKeys, and accept them only after tests and before-and-after benchmarks. In every case, production access for the AI tool is unnecessary.

examPoints: When a Domain 4 stem quotes an error string or a metric name, map it to its layer (permissions, integration, throttling, deployment, capacity) before reading the options.
